events.text: The paulownia by the well was planted the year the youngest daughter of the house was born, as paulownias are: it grows fast, and when she marries it will be cut for her wedding chest. That is next week. The carpenter has already measured it with a string. This morning, at sunrise, you go out for water and stop with the bucket in your hand. Two birds are in the tree. They are as long as a person is tall, mostly tail, in five colours: blue, white, red, black and yellow. They are singing, together, one voice a little behind the other, and the whole yard has gone quiet to listen. Nobody else is up yet.

choices.text: Run and wake the neighbours: they must see this

effects.log: You run from gate to gate shouting. By the time half the village is in the yard in their sleeping clothes, the tree is empty, and the singing is a thread far off over the hills. Everyone saw something. Nobody agrees what. By the evening the upper village says the birds came for the upper village's luck and the lower village says they were plainly looking at the lower village, and that argument will outlive the tree.

choices.text: Put out a dish of your best millet for them

effects.log: You set a dish of millet on the well's edge, the yellow kind, the best in the house. The birds look at it from the branch. They do not come down. They finish their song, rise together and go. The old village teacher, passing with a pipe, sees the full dish and laughs until he has to sit down. "The phoenix does not peck millet," he says. "A thousand li hungry, and not one grain. You have just met the most stubborn creatures under heaven."

choices.text: Say nothing, and at the wedding beg them to spare the tree one more year

effects.log: You say nothing to anyone. At the wedding talks you stand up, red to the ears, and beg the family to cut a different tree, or wait one more year, or buy a chest. They laugh, and then the bride takes your side, and the tree is spared. At the next sunrise the two birds are back on the high branch. They sing, and stop, and one of them turns its head on its long neck and looks straight down at you, for as long as it takes to fill a bucket. Then they sing again.

events.text: The bird-catcher on the hill sets sticks smeared with lime in the bushes, and small birds that land on them stick fast and are sold in cages at the market. You are not supposed to go near the sticks. Today you go near them, because something is shrieking. On the lime, stuck by both feet and one long wing, is a bird you have never seen in any cage: long-necked, with a crest, and a tail of five colours that trails down into the grass. On the branch above, a second bird just like it is walking up and down and calling, and will not fly away. The catcher is coming up the path with an empty cage, whistling.

choices.text: Run to the catcher and offer your two coppers to let it go

effects.log: You hold out the two coppers you were saving for a sugar figure. The catcher looks at the bird on the lime, and at the coins, and at your face, and some old thing in his own face gives way. "Two coppers," he says. "It is worth a hundred taels. Go on." He works it loose himself, with oil, very gently. It flies up to the other bird, and the two of them go over the hill together. The catcher spits, and then laughs, and says he will deny this to anyone.

choices.text: Get lamp oil from home and work the lime off its feet yourself

ok.log: You run home and back with the lamp-oil jar under your shirt and work the lime off its feet and its wing with your fingers, the bird quiet under your hands, the other one watching from above with its head on one side. The catcher comes round the bend just as it flies. He sees only the oil on your hands and a very long feather on the ground, and chases you halfway down the hill, roaring.

fail.log: You are halfway through the second foot when the catcher arrives. He grabs your collar; the bird tears itself loose and leaves three tail feathers in the lime, and flies up to its mate, and they are gone. The catcher boxes your ears and takes you home to your family to be shouted at. You do not mind the shouting. (-4 health)

choices.text: Stand in front of the sticks and do not move

effects.log: You plant yourself in front of the bush with your arms out. The catcher stops and stares at you. While he is deciding whether to laugh, the bird on the lime pulls, hard, and comes free all at once, leaving one long blue feather stuck in the lime, and goes up to its mate. The catcher curses and goes to look for his sticks elsewhere. You peel the blue feather off the lime and keep it in a box under your sleeping mat for the rest of your life.

events.text: {npc}, lord of a small hill kingdom of three valleys, pays well and asks one thing: hang nets. A pair of phoenixes has nested on the ridge above the lord's hall, and the lord's geomancer says the kingdom's luck will last only as long as they stay. So a hundred nets of silk are strung across the ridge, and martial artists are hired to hold them, and you are one. On the third dawn something hits your net like a thrown bolt of cloth. It is one of the pair, five colours, tangled to the neck, very still. The other one circles overhead, crying, and the watchers below start shouting: "Bong! You caught the bong! Good luck!" "No, that is the hwang! Bad luck!"

choices.text: Hold it for the lord: you took the pay

effects.log: You hold the net closed until the lord's men come up with a cage. {npc} is delighted and pays you double, and the bird in the cage does not sing, not once, though the one outside the cage sits on the hall roof every day and sings for both. Within the month the people of the three valleys are arguing about you: whether you caught the good-luck half or the bad-luck half. Nobody ever finds out.

choices.text: Cut your own net and let it go

effects.log: Your knife goes through the silk in three strokes. The bird drops, opens its wings a hand above the rocks and goes up to its mate, and the two of them go over the ridge. The lord's men come for you with clubs; you leave two of them in the heather and take a cut on the arm. {npc} shouts from the hall door that you have stolen a kingdom's luck. You think, walking away, that a kingdom's luck in a net was never luck. (-8 health)

choices.text: Let it go, and come back tonight for the other ninety-nine

ok.log: You free the bird, wait for dark and go along the ridge from net to net with your knife, a hundred times, and by the hour of the tiger there is nothing on the mountain but cut silk blowing like grass. At dawn the two birds are on the highest rock, singing. {npc} stands in the hall yard looking up at them for a long time and does not send anyone after you.

fail.log: You free the bird and come back at night for the rest, and get through sixty nets before the lord's champions find you. It is a hard fight in the dark among the poles, and you go down the far side of the ridge bleeding. But sixty nets is enough of a gap. At dawn, from the next valley, you hear two voices singing on the mountain. (-15 health)

events.text: The people you answer to owe a debt to a hill-king's crown-maker, and the crown-maker wants payment in feathers: five-coloured ones, long, for the standing ornaments of a gilt-bronze crown. You are sent with a purse to the feather-takers' camp in the high pines. Everyone at home thinks these are pheasant feathers dyed. They are not. In the camp, among the drying racks, is a mirror propped against a pine and a dish of millet before it, and a long net, and beside the fire a tied bundle of feathers that still move a little in the wind as if they remember flying. Far up on the ridge two birds are calling to each other, one voice a little behind the other.

choices.text: Buy the feathers, as you were sent to

effects.log: You pay and carry the bundle home wrapped in silk. The crown-maker strokes the feathers with one finger and goes pale, and says nothing about pheasants. The crown is very beautiful. All that year, at dawn, you dream of two voices, and then of one.

choices.text: Follow the takers up the ridge and break their trap

ok.log: You follow them in the dark to the ridge and find the mirror-trap set for the morning: a mirror so a bird sees a rival, millet to shame it, and the net behind. You smash the mirror with your scabbard, scatter the millet and tie the takers to their own poles. At sunrise two birds come down the ridge, look at the broken glass, and go on singing.

fail.log: There are more of them than you counted, and they know the ridge. You break the mirror, but they break two of your ribs before you get away down the scree. In the morning you hear the birds still calling, both of them. That will have to do. (-10 health)

choices.text: Take the feathers and burn them, so nobody wears them

effects.log: You pay, walk a li down the path, and burn the bundle in a ditch. The smoke is five colours for a moment and smells of nothing at all. You go home and say the takers had nothing to sell this year. You have never lied so well, or felt so clean about it.

events.text: A court famous for its virtue has had the ancient music written out again, in nine movements, to call the phoenixes, and you are among the guests of honour in the stone courtyard on the day it is played. The bells, the stone chimes, the pipes, the zithers, the clapper; then the second movement, and the third. At the ninth movement two birds come down out of the clear sky into the courtyard, long-necked, crested, their tails trailing five colours over the flagstones, and they stand in a slow measured dance, as the old books say they did for Shun. The court weeps for joy. Then the birds stop dancing, and turn, and walk past the musicians to you, the only one there strong enough to see what heaven sees: under the throne, a crime, old and buried and real. "We have come," one of them says, in a voice like a pipe of bamboo. "Must we stay?"

choices.text: Testify that the king is worthy: the crime is old, and the reign is good

effects.log: "The crime is under the throne," you say, "not on it. The one who sits there now has fed three famines and opened every prison. Stay." The birds look at each other for a long moment. Then they stay, and the dance begins again, and the court never knows that you were asked anything. Years of peace follow. You will wonder all your life whether you were right.

choices.text: Testify to the crime

effects.log: You tell them, aloud, so the whole court hears: what was done, to whom, and where it is buried. The music falters and stops. The birds rise from the courtyard without a sound, and go, and the court turns to stare at you, and then at the throne. The reign does not fall. But it is never quite the same reign again, and the buried thing is dug up, and given a proper grave.

choices.text: Say that it is not for humans to answer

effects.log: "You came," you say. "Whether you stay is yours. I will not lend you my eyes to make it easier." One of the birds makes a sound very like a laugh. They finish the ninth movement's dance, exactly to the end, and rise, and go. Nobody knows whether that was a blessing or a farewell. You think that was the point.

events.text: Above the clouds, a jade court whose ruler has governed a thousand years without a war has the music of nine movements played on instruments of cloud-stone and sky-bamboo, and you, newly risen, are given a seat in the courtyard to hear it. events.text: {npc}, a keeper of the jade court's music, finds you on a terrace of cloud some years after the day of the nine movements. "The birds come back sometimes," {npc} says. "Only at the ninth movement, and only if someone they have already spoken to is in the courtyard. They have asked for you."

choices.text: Go, and stand in the courtyard again

effects.log: You stand in the courtyard while the nine movements go round. At the ninth the two birds come down and dance, and this time they ask you nothing. One of them, passing, lays the tip of its long tail across your feet for a moment, like a hand on a shoulder. {npc} weeps openly, which you gather is unusual for a keeper of music.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the birds said about you

effects.log: {npc} hesitates. "That you answered," {npc} says at last. "That most people, asked, say what they think heaven wants to hear. That you did not." {npc} bows to you, deeply, and goes back to tune the stone chimes.

events.text: The year of grace for the paulownia by the well is nearly up. The two birds have come to it at sunrise all year, except in the worst of the winter, and the whole household now gets up early on purpose and pretends it has not. The carpenter has come back with his measuring string, and the bride, who has been waiting a year to be married because of you, looks at you across the yard. Everyone looks at you. It was your idea.

choices.text: Ask the carpenter to make the chest from some other wood

effects.log: You pay the difference for a chest of pine out of your own savings. The carpenter grumbles that pine chests warp and the bride's clothes will smell of resin. The bride laughs, and says they will smell of resin and she will think of the birds. The tree stays. The next dawn, two voices.

choices.text: Tell them to cut it: a year was what you asked for

effects.log: The tree comes down on a grey morning when the birds are not there. The chest is light and pale and smells of nothing, which is what paulownia is for. The bride is married from it. On the lid, the village painter puts two birds facing each other, from your description. Neither of them looks right, and the bride loves them.

choices.text: Ask the bride what she wants

effects.log: She thinks about it all evening and in the morning says: cut a branch, only one, the low one the birds never use, and make a small box of it for her hairpins. The rest stays. The carpenter says it is the smallest commission of his life. The box is very beautiful.

events.text: A child is born in the household, a girl, and someone says, as people do, that a paulownia should be planted for her. Everyone turns to you, because of the old tree by the well, which is enormous now and has its two birds at sunrise, some years, as if they never left.

choices.text: Plant a seedling from the old tree's root

effects.log: You dig a root-sucker from under the old tree and plant it by the gate, and water it every morning for a year. It grows as fast as paulownias do. The first time the two birds come down, they go to the old tree. The second time, one of them lands, for a moment, on the young one, and the whole household holds its breath.

choices.text: Plant two, so no tree ever has to be cut alone

effects.log: Two seedlings, one on each side of the gate. Your neighbours laugh, and in a few years every new household in the village is planting its paulownias in pairs, and nobody can remember why, except you.

choices.text: Say that the birds choose their own trees

effects.log: "You cannot plant for them," you say. "You can only plant, and be worth it." The household plants a seedling anyway, as households do. You find you are pleased.

events.text: A war passes near the village, and soldiers camped in the valley are cutting every tree in reach for firewood. An officer with an axe on his shoulder is standing under the paulownias by the gate, looking up, judging how well they will burn.

choices.text: Bring the officer every stick of firewood you own

effects.log: You carry out the household's whole winter store and pile it at the officer's feet. He looks at the pile, and at the trees, and at you, and shrugs, and takes the wood. It is a cold winter. The trees stand.

choices.text: Stand under the trees with your weapon

ok.log: You do not say anything. You do not need to. The officer weighs the trees against you and decides the trees are not worth it, and goes to cut a pine on the hill instead.

fail.log: There are five of them and they want the wood. You fight, and lose, and they cut one tree before their officer, embarrassed, calls them off the other. In the spring a shoot comes up from the stump. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell the officer about the two birds

effects.log: You tell it simply: the daughter's tree, the year of grace, the two birds at sunrise. The officer listens with the axe still on his shoulder. Then he says that his own mother planted a paulownia for his sister, and walks away without a word, and the soldiers cut elsewhere.

events.text: It is three harvests since you ran shouting through the village about the two birds in the paulownia, and the upper and lower villages are still not speaking. A plough-ox has been lent the wrong way, a wedding called off, and this morning somebody's hens were found in the well. Both headmen have come to your gate to ask you, as the one who saw them first, which village the birds were looking at.

choices.text: Say they were looking at nobody: they were singing to each other

effects.log: Both headmen are furious, and then, slowly, a little ashamed. The quarrel does not end that day. But it stops being about luck, and becomes, in a few years, about hens, which can be settled with money.

choices.text: Say they were looking at you

effects.log: It ends the quarrel at once. Both villages agree, with great relief, to be annoyed with you instead. For years nobody lends you an ox. You find this very fair.

choices.text: Call both villages to the tree at dawn, every dawn, until the birds come back

effects.log: It takes forty dawns. Both villages come, grumbling, wrapped in blankets, on opposite sides of the tree. On the forty-first the birds come, and sing, and go, and the two villages find they have been standing together for an hour without noticing, and it is hard to start a quarrel again after that.

events.text: Years later, a traveller at the inn tells a story about two villages that stood together at dawn under a paulownia waiting for two birds, and how the birds came. You were there. The traveller has it nearly all wrong, and has made you into a sage with a white beard.

choices.text: Correct the story

effects.log: You correct it. The traveller is polite, and the room is bored, and the story is worse. That night you hear the traveller telling it again in the yard, with the white beard back in. Stories know what they are doing.

choices.text: Let it stand, and buy the traveller a cup

effects.log: You buy the cup and listen to the end, where the sage says a wise thing you never said. It is a good thing to have said. You decide to start saying it.

events.text: The old teacher who laughed at your dish of millet has not forgotten it. He calls you into the schoolroom one evening and makes you copy out a line, over and over: that the phoenix flies a thousand li hungry and does not peck millet; that it rests only on the paulownia, eats only bamboo seed, drinks only from a sweet spring.

choices.text: Copy it a hundred times, carefully

effects.log: By the hundredth time your hand knows it better than your head does. The teacher reads the last sheet and nods. "Now you will notice," he says, "every time somebody holds out millet to you." You do not understand him until years later.

choices.text: Ask him whether a creature that proud is any use

effects.log: He thinks about it seriously, which you did not expect. "No use at all," he says. "It does not plough, it does not lay, it does not guard. It only refuses. And when it refuses, the whole kingdom learns what it was being offered."

events.text: A merchant who wants the county's salt contract has been told that you have the magistrate's ear. A sack is delivered to your door, very heavy, tied with red string. Inside, under a layer of millet, is silver.

choices.text: Send it back, millet and all

effects.log: You send it back with a note that says only: not one grain. The merchant does not understand the note. The magistrate, who hears of it, does, and laughs, and gives the contract to someone else.

choices.text: Keep the millet, send back the silver

effects.log: You eat the millet that winter, which is very good millet, and return the silver with thanks. The merchant is so confused that he tells the whole county, and the whole county decides you are either a sage or a fool, and stops sending you sacks.

choices.text: Keep it all

effects.log: You keep it. The silver buys a new roof. Every morning that year you wake before dawn for no reason and lie listening, and nothing sings.

events.text: The bird-catcher on the hill is getting old, and has started talking to you when you pass, as if you were partners in something. Today he is sitting on the path with his empty cages. "Since that morning," he says, "I cannot set a stick without seeing that bird on it. I have not caught a thing in a month. What am I supposed to live on?"

choices.text: Help him learn another trade: he knows the hills

effects.log: He knows every herb on the hill and has never thought of selling one. You go with him to the apothecary in town and do the talking. In a year he is the best herb-gatherer in the county, and keeps one lime-stick on his wall, clean, for remembering.

choices.text: Tell him to set his sticks where the small birds are, and leave the high ridge alone

effects.log: He grunts and agrees. He never sets a stick on the high ridge again, and tells every catcher he meets that the high ridge is cursed, which works better than the truth would.

choices.text: Give him your share of the harvest money

effects.log: He takes it with a scowl and buys rice with it. He is not grateful. A month later you find a basket of chestnuts on your doorstep, and then every autumn after.

events.text: You open the box under your sleeping mat, which you have not opened in years. The blue feather is still there, and still blue, as bright as the morning on the lime. Everything else in the box has faded. You hold it up to the light and it seems, very faintly, to lean toward the east.

choices.text: Carry it with you from now on

effects.log: You sew it into the lining of your jacket. It weighs nothing. Over the years you notice that you never get lost walking east, and that you can always tell, somehow, when someone is lying to you about a gift.

choices.text: Put it back: it is safer in the box

effects.log: You put it back. The next time you open the box it has turned to point east again, and you decide not to think about that.

events.text: {npc}, the lord of the three valleys, sends word to you, under a promise of safe passage, a year after the morning of the nets. The hall is quieter than you remember. "The geomancer has gone," {npc} says. "The harvest failed in one valley and doubled in the other. I do not know if I have luck or not. You were there. Tell me what I had in my net."

choices.text: Say: a guest, not a fortune

effects.log: {npc} is quiet for a long time. "A guest," {npc} says. "I put a net round a guest." The next spring the nets are taken down and burned, and the lord's own hand plants paulownias on the ridge, a long row of them, for no one in particular.

choices.text: Say: whatever it was, it is gone, so rule as if you never had it

effects.log: {npc} laughs, for the first time in a year. It is good advice for any lord, it turns out. The three valleys are well governed after that, and nobody can say whether it was luck.

choices.text: Say nothing, take the fee and go

effects.log: {npc} pays you to say something, and you do not, and leave. You hear later that a new geomancer is hanging new nets. You do not go back.

events.text: The bird you held for the lord sits in its cage in the hall yard, five colours gone dull. It has not sung in years. Its mate still comes to the roof at dawn. Tonight you are on watch in the yard, alone, with the key to the cage on your belt, because the lord trusts you.

choices.text: Open the cage

effects.log: The door swings. The bird does not move for a long time, as if it has forgotten. Then it walks out, and stretches its neck, and goes up to the roof in one long beat of its wings, and in the morning there is a song from the ridge that the whole hill kingdom hears. You are gone by then, and the key is hanging on the cage door.

choices.text: Leave it: you were paid, and the lord trusts you

effects.log: You keep the watch. In the morning the mate sings on the roof, alone, for both of them, and you find you cannot stay in the yard to hear it, and ask to be put on the gate.

events.text: On the road, an old martial artist who held one of the hundred nets that year falls in beside you. "I heard you cut yours," the old one says. "I wanted to. I held mine shut and was paid and drank it. I still think about the sound the second bird made."

choices.text: Say that cutting cost you nothing worth having

effects.log: It cost you a cut arm and a job and a lord's hatred, but you say it anyway, and find it is true. The old one walks with you to the next town and buys you rice, and does not talk about it again.

choices.text: Say that the second bird is still singing on that ridge, both of them

effects.log: The old one stops in the road. "Both?" Yes. Both. The old martial artist sits down on a milestone and laughs, and wipes both eyes, and you leave them there, lighter.

events.text: The hill-king wears the feathered crown at the spring rites, and the whole hill kingdom comes to see it. The feathers you bought shine on it like a rainbow caught in metal. Behind you in the crowd an old woman says, quite loudly, that no bird gives up feathers like that while it is alive.

choices.text: Go to the crown-maker and tell what the feathers are

effects.log: The crown-maker already knows. "I knew when I touched them," the crown-maker says. "I made it anyway, because the king pays." You both sit in the workshop for a long time without speaking. The next crown the workshop makes is gilt and nothing else.

choices.text: Go up into the hills and look for the birds

ok.log: It takes a season. On a ridge above the pines you hear it at dawn: one voice, and then, after a long while, another, answering. Both alive. You sit on the rock and cry for no reason you could explain to anybody.

fail.log: You search a season and hear only one voice, at dawn, on every ridge, the same one, calling and not answered. You go home and do not talk about the crown again.

events.text: The feather-takers whose trap you broke, or whose feathers you burned, have not forgotten you. One of them is waiting on the pass with a net over one shoulder and a grin. "You cost us a season," the taker says. "We have a mirror again. Want to see what it shows you?"

choices.text: Fight

ok.log: It is a short fight. You break the mirror over your knee afterwards and throw the pieces off the pass, where they flash in the sun all the way down.

fail.log: The taker is better than the grin suggested. You get away with the net round one ankle and the mirror cracked, at least. (-12 health)

choices.text: Offer to pay the season back

effects.log: The taker stares, and then counts the silver very carefully, and says that a season is a season, and goes. You think that was cheap.

choices.text: Look in the mirror

effects.log: You look. It shows you, as mirrors do, yourself: a person who has had to choose, more than once, between the pay and the bird. The taker laughs and goes. You stand on the pass a long time.

events.text: The king of the nine movements sends for you, privately, at night. There is no one else in the room. "They spoke to you," the king says. "Everyone saw them turn. Nobody heard. I have not slept since. Tell me what they asked, and what you said."

choices.text: Tell the king the truth, all of it

effects.log: You tell it. The king listens with both hands flat on the table, and at the end gets up and walks out of the room, and you hear the king's footsteps going down, and down, to whatever is under the throne. In the morning the court is told of an old crime and an old grave, by the king's own mouth. It is the most courageous thing you have seen a ruler do.

choices.text: Say only: they asked whether to stay

effects.log: "And what did you say?" You look at the king and do not answer. The king nods, slowly, as if that were an answer. It probably is.

choices.text: Say that it was between you and them

effects.log: The king's face goes through anger and fear and settles on something like respect. "Then I will have to be worth it without knowing," the king says. "As everyone else is."

events.text: A child at the palace gate, a musician's apprentice, stops you as you pass. "You were in the courtyard at the ninth movement," the child says. "My teacher was the flautist. My teacher's flute was out of tune and my teacher wept. My teacher thinks the birds came in spite of the flute. Did they?"

choices.text: Say they came because of it

effects.log: "A flute that weeps is in tune with something," you say. You are not sure it is true. The child runs off with it, and you hear later that the old flautist played again, badly and gladly, for twenty more years.

choices.text: Say you did not notice the flute at all

effects.log: The child looks disappointed, then delighted. "Then nobody did," the child says, and goes off to tell the teacher, who, you hear, laughs for the first time in a month.

events.text: Many years after the nine movements, travelling, you come through the old kingdom of that court. In a hillside village someone has painted the courtyard scene on the wall of the shrine: the musicians, the two birds, the king. And at the edge of the picture, small, a figure standing a little apart. People are bowing to that figure. The shrine-keeper tells you it is heaven's witness.

choices.text: Tell the keeper it was only you

effects.log: The keeper looks at you, and at the painted figure, and decides very firmly that you are mistaken. You are given a cup of tea and asked to leave a donation for the witness. You leave one.

choices.text: Bow to the painted figure too

effects.log: You bow to yourself, small and painted on a wall. It feels exactly as strange as you expected and also, unexpectedly, like setting something down.

events.text: A woman of the household, heavy with child, wakes everyone before dawn with a dream. A bird came down out of five-coloured clouds, she says, long-necked, its tail sweeping the sky; it flew into her arms and would not let go however she pulled. Then she saw there had been two of them, and the other was watching from a branch. By breakfast the whole lane knows. By noon there is an argument: was it the bong, and the child will be one thing, or the hwang, and the child will be another?

choices.text: Say a dream like that does not choose between bong and hwang

effects.log: "There were two of them," you point out. "It came with its mate. It does not care what the baby is." The lane is disappointed. The mother-to-be, who has been listening, takes your hand and holds it a long time.

choices.text: Go to the fortune-teller and pay for a proper reading

effects.log: The fortune-teller reads it with great confidence and is, it turns out later, exactly half right, which is the best anyone ever does with a phoenix.

choices.text: Keep quiet and write the dream down exactly

effects.log: You write it down on a sheet of mulberry paper with the date, every word she said, and fold it into the rafters. Somebody, someday, should have it exactly.

events.text: The child of the phoenix dream is born, and is entirely ordinary: red, furious and loud. The lane is let down. The child's grandmother wants the dream kept a secret from the child forever, so the child will not grow up proud; the child's uncle wants it told every night.

choices.text: Side with the grandmother

effects.log: The dream is kept. The child grows up proud anyway, about other things, as children do.

choices.text: Side with the uncle

effects.log: The child hears the dream every night and grows up looking up at every bird. It is not a bad way to grow up.

choices.text: Say it should be told once, when the child is grown

effects.log: Everyone agrees, with relief, to leave it to you. You did not mean that. Still, the paper in the rafters is waiting.

events.text: The child of the phoenix dream is grown, about to leave the village for good, and has come to you because somebody said you have something to tell. The paper is still folded in the rafters, a little yellow now.

choices.text: Give the paper

effects.log: The grown child reads it twice and laughs and cries at the same time. "Two of them," the young one says. "It came with its mate." Something settles in that face that you had not known was unsettled.

choices.text: Tell it in your own words, and keep the paper

effects.log: You tell it, and add nothing. The young one listens, nods, and goes. Years later a letter comes from a far province: the young one has planted a paulownia, two of them, by a schoolhouse.

events.text: It is a hard winter and you have been feeding the sparrows from your own bowl, a pinch of millet every morning on the frozen yard. This morning there is a stranger among them: a bird far too big and far too long in the tail, thin, its feathers dull with cold, its five colours barely showing. It looks at the millet and does not touch it.

choices.text: Push the millet closer to it

effects.log: It steps back from the millet as if from a fire, and flies up into the bare paulownia, and stays there all morning, starving and calm. You do not understand, and you think about it for years.

choices.text: Find it something else: the dried bamboo seed in the storehouse

ok.log: There is a little bag of bamboo seed, years old, that someone gathered in a flowering year as a curiosity. You scatter it on the snow. The thin bird comes down at once and eats every grain, and looks at you, and goes. In spring, two of them sing from the paulownia.

fail.log: You turn the storehouse over and find nothing it will eat: not rice, not barley, not beans. By the time you come back it is gone. You keep a little of everything in your pocket all winter, just in case.

choices.text: Let it be, and feed the sparrows

effects.log: The sparrows eat. The big bird watches from the paulownia. When you go in, a sparrow lands beside it on the branch and seems, for all the world, to be scolding it.

events.text: The thin bird of that winter has come back, fat and brilliant, with its mate, and they are in the paulownia every dawn this spring. The sparrows have decided the two of them are their kings. You have decided nothing, but the village children follow you about asking whether the birds will grant wishes.

choices.text: Say they grant nothing, but they remember

effects.log: The children are disappointed and then thrilled. Remembering is better than wishes; wishes are over in a moment. They spend the rest of the spring being remembered at, very carefully.

choices.text: Make up a wish for each child

effects.log: Twenty wishes, all small and possible: a new top, a kind word from a sister, snow on New Year. A surprising number come true. You do not take credit.

events.text: In the market a man in a frayed scholar's hat keeps asking the poultry seller next to the stall where you are shopping about one big red cock in the basket. "Is that a phoenix?" he asks. "No," says the seller. An hour later: "Surely that is a phoenix." "No." Another hour. By evening the tired seller says, "Yes, fine, it is a phoenix," and the man pays ten times a cock's price on the spot and walks off with it under his arm, toward the magistrate's office.

choices.text: Warn the seller: this is a trap

effects.log: The seller does not listen; the silver is too heavy in the hand. You watch the man walk into the magistrate's gate with the bird held up high, announcing a phoenix for the magistrate.

choices.text: Follow the man and see what happens

effects.log: He gives the cock to the magistrate as a phoenix, a gift. The magistrate looks at a cock. The man is beaten with the paddle for mockery, ten strokes, and comes out limping and grinning, and goes straight back toward the market.

choices.text: Mind your own errands

effects.log: You mind your errands. It is no business of yours. You do notice the man coming back at dusk, limping, and grinning very wide.

events.text: The man in the frayed hat is back at the poultry stall, limping, demanding his money back: ten times a cock's price, he says, and the price of the beating as well, because the seller swore before witnesses it was a phoenix. He points at you. "You heard!"

choices.text: Testify that the seller said it

effects.log: It is true; the seller said it. The magistrate, weary, makes the seller pay. The man in the frayed hat walks away richer than he came, with a bow to you. You feel used and also, oddly, that you have learned something about the word "phoenix".

choices.text: Testify that everybody knew it was a cock

effects.log: "Nobody in the market thought it was a phoenix," you say, "including the buyer." The magistrate laughs and throws the case out. The man in the frayed hat tips the hat to you, entirely without malice, and is gone from the county by morning.

choices.text: Say that a real phoenix would never be in a basket

effects.log: The magistrate looks up. "And how would you know?" You tell him what the old people say: it does not peck millet, it does not sit in a basket, it does not come when it is called. The magistrate dismisses the case and asks you to stay for tea, and asks about phoenixes until dark.

events.text: You have hired on with a bird-catcher for the season: lime-sticks, nets, cages, a share of what sells. The master catcher has one rule, said every morning: "If you ever see two long-tailed birds of five colours, take your sticks down and walk away. Do not catch them. Do not look at them long." Today, on the high ridge, you see them.
events.arc: The Two Birds Not to Catch

choices.text: Take your sticks down and walk away

effects.log: You pull every stick, wrap them, and walk back down without looking up. Behind you the two birds sing, and the sound follows you all the way to the bottom of the hill. The master catcher, when you tell it, nods and says nothing and gives you a full share for the day anyway.

choices.text: Look at them long

effects.log: You look until your neck aches. Five colours, and on each bird, if you squint, shapes in the feathers like old characters: one on the head, one on the wings, one on the back, one on the breast, one on the belly. You cannot read them. You cannot stop trying.

choices.text: Set a stick, quietly: the price of one would make you rich

ok.log: The bird lands near the stick, looks at it, looks at you, and lands somewhere else. All day. At evening you find a single long feather on your lime, given, not taken, you think. You sell it for five taels and feel worse than if you had caught nothing.

fail.log: You climb to set the stick and the branch breaks. You come down through the pine in a shower of needles, and the two birds watch you hit the ground, and leave. (-6 health)

events.text: Late in the season the master catcher gets drunk on the last night and tells you why. Forty years ago, young, the master caught one of the two. It was sold to a governor's household for a fortune. The other one followed the cart to the governor's gate and sat on the roof and sang, every dawn, for a year, and then did not sing again.
events.arc: The Two Birds Not to Catch

choices.text: Ask what happened to the one in the cage

effects.log: "It never ate," the master catcher says. "They offered it the best millet in the province. It would not touch millet. It died in the spring. The governor's house had bad luck for a generation, and I had a fortune, and I would give it back."

choices.text: Ask why the master still catches birds at all

effects.log: "Because sparrows sell," the master says, "and nobody hangs a kingdom's luck on a sparrow." It is not a good answer, and you both know it, and you raise your tea to it anyway.

choices.text: Say nothing, and pour

effects.log: You pour, and the master talks until dawn, and at dawn you hear, far up on the ridge, two voices. The master catcher hears them too, and puts down the cup.

events.text: Years later, a feather-dealer from the hill kingdoms comes looking for the catcher you once worked for, and finds you instead. The dealer wants someone who knows the high ridge, and has a mirror wrapped in cloth and a sack of millet. "A mirror," the dealer says, "so it sees a rival. Millet, to shame it. Lead me to the ridge and name your price."
events.arc: The Two Birds Not to Catch

choices.text: Lead the dealer to the wrong ridge

effects.log: You lead the dealer three days the wrong way, to a ridge with nothing on it but crows, and take your fee, and wish the dealer luck. The dealer never comes back to the county.

choices.text: Refuse and warn the catchers

effects.log: Every catcher in the county hears of the mirror-trap by the next market day. Nobody will sell the dealer so much as a sparrow. The dealer leaves, cursing your whole county by name.

choices.text: Take the money and lead the dealer true

effects.log: You lead the dealer true. You do not stay to see the trap work. For the rest of your life, at dawn, you hear only one voice on any ridge, and you cannot tell anyone why that bothers you.

events.text: Somebody's big red rooster flew up onto the roof of the village shrine on the morning a traveller swore they saw a phoenix pass over, and now half the village says the rooster is the phoenix in disguise. It is being fed rice cakes and given red string. It has become impossible.

choices.text: Climb up and bring it down

ok.log: You bring it down by the legs, squawking. It pecks you twice and the village gasps at the sacrilege. Then it is just a rooster again, standing in the yard, very offended. The village goes home slightly ashamed.

fail.log: The rooster does not want to come down and you discover how sharp a rooster's spurs are. The village decides this proves it is a phoenix. (-5 health)

choices.text: Point out that a phoenix does not eat rice cakes

effects.log: The old people go quiet and nod. The young people do not know the saying. You tell it to them: not millet, not rice, only bamboo seed. By evening the rooster's cult has lost half its members and the rooster has gained a great deal of weight.

choices.text: Let it be: it does no harm

effects.log: It does no harm. It does lay claim to the shrine roof for the rest of its life and crow from it at the hour of the tiger, every single day, which some people consider harm.

events.text: The shrine rooster has died of old age and great honour, and the village wants to bury it with rites. And this morning, on the paulownia at the top of the village, a real one is sitting: long-necked, five colours, quiet, looking down at the funeral procession.

choices.text: Point it out to everyone

effects.log: Every head turns. The real bird looks back at them, sings three notes, and goes. The village buries the rooster anyway, with rites, and nobody laughs, because you never know.

choices.text: Watch it alone and say nothing

effects.log: Nobody else looks up. The bird watches the whole procession go by, the drum and the little coffin, and when it is over it lifts its head and sings once, very low, as if for the rooster, and leaves.

events.text: On the road you sleep under a huge paulownia on a hilltop, and wake at dawn to singing. Above you on a branch is a bird the length of a spear, five colours, singing to the sunrise. You have a bundle of rice balls. It is looking at them.

choices.text: Offer it a rice ball

effects.log: You hold one up. The bird looks at it with what you would swear is great politeness, and does not take it. It finishes its song. You eat the rice ball yourself, and it is the best rice ball you have ever eaten, for no reason.

choices.text: Eat, and listen

effects.log: You eat slowly, so as not to make noise. The song goes on until the sun is clear of the hills. When it stops, you find that the old wound in your shoulder that aches every dawn has not ached at all.

choices.text: Practise your forms in the sunrise beside it

effects.log: You practise the opening forms in the red light. The bird watches with its head on one side. Once, when you get a turn exactly right, it sings a single note, and you find yourself doing that turn again and again for an hour to make it sing again.

events.text: You come back by the same road a year later, and the paulownia on the hilltop is still there. Under it, on a flat stone, someone has left a little heap of bamboo seed, as if for a guest. The bird is not there. A farmer in the field below says it comes every spring now, with its mate, and that the spring on the hill has started to taste of rice wine.

choices.text: Add to the heap from your own pack

effects.log: You have no bamboo seed. You leave a coin, which is useless to a phoenix, and a rice ball, which is useless too. You leave them anyway. The farmer watches you and laughs, and then, after you have gone, leaves one too.

choices.text: Drink from the spring

effects.log: It is cold and faintly sweet, like the first cup at a wedding. You fill your gourd. It stays sweet for a month and then, the day you lie to a gatekeeper about your name, turns to ordinary water.

events.text: {npc}, the geomancer of a small hill kingdom, has hired you as an escort for a survey of the ridges. On the third day, on a spur above the king's hall, {npc} stops, sets down the compass board and goes pale. "The land is shaped like a nesting bird," {npc} says. "Phoenix ground. If two of them ever come here, this kingdom's luck will hang on their staying." Then, more quietly: "And kings who hang their luck on birds start buying nets."

choices.text: Say {npc} should tell the king nothing

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time. "A geomancer who keeps a secret from a king," {npc} says. "That is how geomancers die." But the survey report, when it is written, says the spur is good for pine and nothing else.

choices.text: Say {npc} should tell the king everything, nets included

effects.log: {npc} tells the king, nets included, and the king listens to the part about the nets. There will be no nets, the king says. You hope it is a king who remembers saying things.

choices.text: Ask whether there is any ground that is not shaped like something

effects.log: {npc} laughs, startled. "No," {npc} says. "That is the whole trouble with my trade. Every hill is a dragon or a bird or a boat if you want it to be." You walk on with the compass board between you, and {npc} is much better company after that.

events.text: Two birds have come to the spur above the hill-king's hall: five colours, long tails, singing at sunrise. The king is beside himself with joy, and you are sent for, as the escort who was there at the survey, and told to guard the spur so nobody disturbs them. The court's young officers are already arguing about nets.

choices.text: Guard the spur from the court as well

effects.log: You let nobody up, not the officers, not their bird-catchers, not, once, the crown prince with a bow. The two birds sing every morning that year. The king is told it is because of the guard. The king may be right.

choices.text: Guard it, and let the officers hang their nets lower down

effects.log: It seems a fair compromise until the morning one bird swoops low over the slope and comes away from the nets with a torn wing. The pair leave the spur that week and do not come back.

choices.text: Advise the king to plant paulownias, not hang nets

effects.log: The king laughs and then does it: a whole slope of saplings below the spur. They grow fast, as paulownias do. When you are old, someone tells you the slope is still called the Escort's Planting.

events.text: {npc}, the old geomancer, is dying, and has asked for you. "I lied once on that survey," {npc} says. "The spur is phoenix ground, yes. But the valley below is shaped like a boat. A kingdom that keeps phoenixes there out of pride will sink with them in it. I never told anyone that half."

choices.text: Promise to tell the next king

effects.log: You promise. {npc} closes both eyes and smiles. When you tell the next king, years later, the king does not believe you, but remembers, and when bad years come, does not hang a single net.

choices.text: Ask why {npc} never told it

effects.log: "Because a boat can sail a long time," {npc} says, "if nobody drills a hole in it. I did not want to be the one to give them the drill." You sit until the lamp goes out.

events.text: The bamboo of the whole southern hillside has flowered at once, pale and strange, for the first time in anyone's life. The old people are frightened: when bamboo flowers, they say, the grove dies, and then the rats come. The young people have seen something in the grove at dawn, gathering the falling seed: long-necked, five colours, not afraid of anybody.

choices.text: Organise the village to store grain against the rats

effects.log: It is hard work and nobody thanks you: jars sealed with clay, granaries raised on stones, cats borrowed from three villages. The rats come the next year, out of the dying grove in a grey tide. Your village loses a tenth of its grain. The next valley loses half.

choices.text: Go up to the grove at dawn and see the bird

effects.log: It is there, among the stalks, and another one just like it, gathering seed into a hollow tree. They see you and do not leave. For a whole morning you watch two creatures doing the one thing in the world they are made for. The grove is already yellowing at the edges.

choices.text: Gather the bamboo seed to sell as a curiosity

effects.log: Bamboo seed fetches a good price from apothecaries in a flowering year. You gather sacks of it. At dawn the next day, every place where you gathered is the one place in the grove the birds avoid.

events.text: The rats have come out of the dead bamboo into the villages, as the old people said, and the granaries are emptying. A family down the valley is starving. And up in a hollow tree on the hillside, the two birds have a store of bamboo seed that would feed that family through the winter. You know exactly where it is.

choices.text: Leave the birds' store alone and share your own grain

effects.log: You carry three sacks of your own down the valley on your back. It leaves you thin by spring. The family lives. You never tell them about the hollow tree; it is not yours to tell.

choices.text: Take a little from the birds' store

effects.log: You take a little, only a little. The family eats it and lives. The birds come back at dusk, and stand by the hollow tree for a long time, and then fly to another hillside. You do not see them again.

choices.text: Hunt the rats instead, all winter, granary by granary

ok.log: A martial artist hunting rats: the valley laughs, and then the valley stops laughing and starts feeding you, because the granaries you guard stop emptying. By spring you are known in three villages as the Rat General, which you pretend to hate.

fail.log: There are too many. You kill rats till your arms ache and the granaries empty anyway, only slower. You are bitten more times than you can count, and run a fever at the end of it. (-6 health)

events.text: Ten years after the flowering, the dead hillside is green again: young bamboo, thin as reeds. The village children have never seen a flowering and do not believe you. One of them asks whether the long-tailed birds will come back when it flowers again.

choices.text: Say: in sixty years, perhaps a hundred

effects.log: The child works out how old that is and is horrified. "You will be dead!" Very likely. The child promises, gravely, to watch for both of you.

choices.text: Say: they never really left; they are on another hillside, waiting

effects.log: The child goes up the hill every dawn for a month to look. On the last morning the child comes down running, shouting about a song from very far away. You decide to believe it.

events.text: The court has hired you to guard the courtyard while the musicians rehearse the old music in nine movements, which has not been played in two hundred years. The scholars rebuilt it from books: bronze bells and stone chimes, a wooden box struck to begin and a wooden tiger scraped down its back to end. Today, in the seventh movement, every bird in the palace trees goes silent at once.

choices.text: Look up at once

effects.log: There is nothing in the sky. But high on the ridge of the main hall's roof, where nothing was a moment ago, there is the tip of a long tail, five colours, hanging down over the tiles. It is gone before the eighth movement starts.

choices.text: Keep your eyes on the gate, as you were paid to

effects.log: You watch the gate, and so you are the only one who sees the old gatekeeper, at the seventh movement, kneel down on the stones and press both hands together, facing the main hall's roof. You do not turn round. You will always wonder.

choices.text: Tell the musicians to play on, whatever happens

effects.log: The music master looks at you as if you had said something holy. They play on into the eighth movement, the ninth, the wooden tiger scraped to end. Nothing comes. But at the end the music master stands for a long time with eyes closed, listening to the silence of the birds.

events.text: The night before the music is to be played for the king, a court official comes to your post at the gate with a small bag of millet, soaked in something that smells of herbs and sleep. "If they come," the official says, "they must stay. Put this in the courtyard after the ninth movement. They will sleep, and the king will have them always."

choices.text: Throw the bag in the well, in front of the official

effects.log: It hits the water with a soft sound. The official turns white and then red and leaves without a word, and the next morning is not at the music. You are not at the music either: you have been dismissed. You hear, from the street, the ninth movement end.

choices.text: Take it, and give it to the music master

effects.log: The music master smells it, goes very quiet, and takes it straight to the king. The official is gone from court within the week. "The phoenix does not peck millet," the music master says to you afterwards. "Drugged or not. But it would have known we tried."

choices.text: Take the bag and do nothing with it

effects.log: You keep the bag in your sleeve all through the music. Nothing comes at the ninth movement. You wonder, for the rest of your life, whether they knew it was there.

events.text: {npc}, master of a rising sect, has had a banner made with a five-coloured bird on it and wants the real one to bless the founding of the new hall. "The omen," {npc} calls it. {npc} has heard you know where a pair nests and offers you an elder's seat if you bring them to the ceremony, "by whatever means".

choices.text: Refuse: they come to the worthy, or they do not come

effects.log: {npc} smiles thinly. "Then I shall be worthy," {npc} says. The founding goes ahead under the painted banner. Nothing comes. The disciples whisper about it for a generation, and some of them, you hear, become better than their master because of it.

choices.text: Say you will ask them, and go and sit under their tree for a month

effects.log: You sit under the paulownia a month, saying nothing to anyone. On the last morning one of the birds lands near you and looks at you, and then looks away, toward the sect's mountain, and does not go. That is an answer. You go back and tell {npc} so, exactly.

choices.text: Take the offer and set a net

ok.log: You set it, and they never come near it, as if they can read a net from a mountain away. {npc} pays you for trying and gives the elder's seat to someone else. You are relieved, and ashamed of being relieved.

fail.log: You set the net, and in the dark you get your own foot caught in it and hang upside down from a pine until dawn, when the two birds come and sing in the tree beside you, unbothered, and go. (-8 health)

events.text: Years later {npc} sends for you. The sect is large now, and rich, and {npc} is old. "The banner," {npc} says, pointing to it, faded on the hall wall. "They never came. I built all this to be worth one visit from two birds. Was it all for nothing?"

choices.text: Say it was not for nothing: look at the disciples

effects.log: {npc} looks out at the yard, where three hundred young people are practising in the dawn. "Yes," {npc} says, "I suppose they will do." The next week, by chance or not, two birds pass over the sect at dawn, high up, and do not stop. {npc} sees them, and weeps, and is content.

choices.text: Say they do not come to the builders; they come to the built

effects.log: {npc} is silent a long time. Then {npc} takes down the banner with both hands and gives it to the youngest disciple in the hall, and retires that winter to a hut with a single paulownia beside it.

events.text: {npc}, a poor scholar who keeps a village schoolhouse, planted a paulownia by its window thirty years ago, "to see the phoenix", as the old song says. The tree is enormous now. The phoenix has never come. You, passing through, are offered a bowl of thin soup and a seat at the window, and {npc} asks, very shyly, whether someone as strong as you has ever seen one.

choices.text: Tell {npc} the truth: you have, or have heard of them

effects.log: {npc} listens to every word, both hands around the empty bowl, and asks you to describe the tail three times. At the end {npc} looks out at the tree and says, "Then they are real. Then it is only that I am not yet worth it." You want to argue. You cannot find the argument.

choices.text: Say you have not, but you will tell them about the tree if you do

effects.log: {npc} laughs at that until there are tears, and makes you promise properly, with a cup of rice wine poured on the root of the tree. You promise. You find that you mean it.

choices.text: Ask why {npc} keeps waiting

effects.log: "Because a paulownia is a question," {npc} says. "Planting it is asking. If I cut it down, I have stopped asking. I would rather be the one who asked." You sit at the window until the moon is in the branches.

events.text: A letter in {npc}'s careful hand reaches you: the schoolhouse has twelve students this year, the most ever, and the magistrate wants the paulownia by the window cut, for a zither for the magistrate's own daughter. {npc} writes that it is only a tree, and asks you not to trouble yourself.

choices.text: Go to the magistrate

ok.log: You talk to the magistrate for an afternoon about zithers and trees and the old song, and the magistrate, who turns out to have learned the song as a child, sends for a zither from the capital instead. {npc} writes to thank you in the most elaborate characters you have ever seen.

fail.log: The magistrate is not moved by songs. In the end you buy the zither yourself, from a maker two counties away, and send it with your compliments. The tree stays. {npc} never knows what it cost.

choices.text: Write back: a tree that asks is not only a tree

effects.log: You write it, and {npc} reads it aloud to the twelve students, and the students go to the magistrate's gate, all twelve, and stand there in a row all day without saying anything. The magistrate gives up on the zither.

events.text: {npc} has died, the old scholar of the schoolhouse, still waiting. You come for the burial. That night you sit at the window where {npc} sat, and the moon comes up and hangs in the empty branches of the paulownia exactly as in the old song: the bright moon on the empty branch.

choices.text: Write three lines for {npc}

effects.npcPass: old age, still waiting at the schoolhouse
effects.log: You write them on the schoolhouse wall by lamplight. They are not good lines. The children learn them anyway, and their children, and they get better every time they are said.

choices.text: Stay until dawn

effects.npcPass: old age, still waiting at the schoolhouse
effects.log: You stay until dawn, and at dawn something moves in the paulownia, high up: a long tail, five colours, and then another. They sing once, very low, toward the new grave on the hill. You do not tell anyone. You do not need to.

events.text: Passing the old schoolhouse years after the scholar's death, you find it full: thirty children on the porch, a new teacher, a new roof. The paulownia is enormous. In its branches, every spring now, the villagers say, two birds come and stay the season. Nobody remembers why the tree was planted, except the three lines on the wall.

choices.text: Sit in on a lesson

effects.log: The lesson is the three lines. The children chant them with great confidence and complete misunderstanding. The teacher apologises to you for the noise. You say it is the best noise you have heard in years.

choices.text: Leave money for the school, and go

effects.log: You leave it with the new teacher, who tries to refuse. A long tail hangs down from the paulownia over your head as you go out of the gate. You do not look up. You do not need to.

events.text: The capital of an old southern kingdom is full of labourers heaping up earth into great round mounds, each the size of a hill. A geomancer from the north has told the king the capital is a phoenix's nest, and that if eggs are built for it, the phoenix will never leave and the kingdom never fall. The king, who is frightened of his own decline, has believed it. You were hired to guard the geomancer.

choices.text: Watch the geomancer closely

effects.log: The geomancer walks the city at night, alone, pacing it out like a carpenter. You follow at a distance. In a chestnut grove by the river the geomancer stops, kneels and lays a palm flat on the ground, and you hear the geomancer laugh, very quietly, the way a thief laughs.

choices.text: Carry earth with the labourers

effects.log: You carry baskets with them for a season. They are proud of the mounds. They sing as they heap them. You find yourself proud too, and cannot quite say why that frightens you.

choices.text: Ask the geomancer straight out what the land is really shaped like

ok.log: The geomancer looks at you a long time, amused. "A boat," the geomancer says at last. "The mounds are cargo. Every boat has a hold." You do not understand until much later what you were told, and by whom.

fail.log: "A nest," the geomancer says, smiling. "What else?" You are moved to guard the gate after that, and do not get close again.

events.text: The night before the geomancer is to leave the capital with the king's gifts, you find a well freshly dug in the chestnut grove by the river, deep and dark, where there was no well before. The geomancer is packing in a hurry. A capital shaped like a boat, and a hole in its bottom.

choices.text: Stop the geomancer at the gate

ok.log: You stop the geomancer at the gate with the sun coming up. The well is filled in that week, with the king's own shovel the first in. Whether a kingdom can be sunk with a well, you will never know. It is not sunk that year, or the next.

fail.log: The geomancer is far stronger than any geomancer has a right to be, and leaves you in the gate's shadow with your ears ringing, and is gone north by dawn. The well stays. (-12 health)

choices.text: Fill in the well yourself, tonight

effects.log: You fill it alone with a borrowed spade, all night, until your hands bleed. The geomancer leaves at dawn without a look back, as if the well no longer mattered. Maybe it did not. Maybe it was always going to be the mounds.

choices.text: Let it be: kingdoms fall

effects.log: You let the geomancer go. Within your lifetime the old kingdom bows to a northern one without a war. The great mounds are still there, and children slide down them in winter. You go and look at them sometimes.

events.text: An old woman sweeping the top of one of the great earth mounds of the fallen capital says that once, when she was small, she saw a long-tailed bird of five colours sitting on this very mound at dawn, as if on an egg. "It stayed all through the bad years," she says. "It should not have. It was waiting for something that could not hatch."

choices.text: Ask where it went

effects.log: "Nowhere," she says. "It stayed. It stayed until the kingdom went. And then one morning it was not there." She goes on sweeping. You stand on the mound a long time.

choices.text: Help her sweep

effects.log: You sweep together until the mound is clean. At the top, in the grass, you find a feather, long and faded, that might once have been five colours. She tells you to keep it. You do.

events.text: {npc}, court musician to a small kingdom wedged between two great ones, has made a zither of twelve silk strings over a body of a single piece of paulownia, and wants to tune it, not by the old pitch-pipes, but to the voice of the bird that sings on the hill above the capital at dawn. {npc} needs someone strong enough to sit still on the cold hilltop with the instrument for a season and keep the wolves off.

choices.text: Sit the season out with {npc}

effects.log: Every dawn the bird sings, and {npc} turns a bridge under one string a hair's breadth, and listens, and turns it back. By the end of the season the zither has twelve notes and every one of them is the bird's. When {npc} plays it in the capital, half the court weeps and does not know why.

choices.text: Argue: a bird does not sing in the court's scale

effects.log: "Exactly," {npc} says. "That is why." You stay anyway. The zither, when it is done, cannot play half the court's music. It plays the other half better than anything you have heard.

events.text: The small kingdom is falling. One of the great neighbours is at the walls. {npc} comes to you at night with the zither wrapped in silk and twelve rolls of music. "The king that is coming," {npc} says, "loves music. I can go over to that court and the music will live. Or I can stay and burn with the rest. Is music a traitor?"

choices.text: Take {npc} over the wall to the conqueror's court

effects.log: You take {npc} over the wall at the hour of the ox, the zither on your back. The conqueror's court receives the music like rain. {npc} is called a traitor at home and a master abroad, and teaches until death, and the twelve strings are still being played a thousand years later.

choices.text: Say: stay, and play on the wall until the end

effects.log: {npc} plays on the wall all through the last night. The besiegers stop to listen. At dawn the gate is opened, without a fight, by a minister who could not bear it. {npc} survives, by a hair, and plays for the conqueror after all, but having stayed.

choices.text: Say: music is not anybody's, so it cannot betray anybody

effects.log: {npc} looks at the zither a long time and then nods. You go over the wall together. On the hill above the capital, as you pass, a bird sings at dawn: twelve notes, every one of them on the strings.

events.text: In the conqueror's capital, years later, you hear a zither of twelve strings being played in a courtyard, by a student of {npc}'s student. It is not tuned to the court's scale. Above the courtyard, on the roof ridge of the hall, something long-tailed and five-coloured is sitting, listening.

choices.text: Go in and listen

effects.log: You stand at the back of the courtyard. The student plays badly and with great love. The bird on the roof listens to the end and goes. Nobody but you looked up.

choices.text: Ask the student who the music came from

effects.log: The student tells you a story about {npc} in which almost everything is wrong and the music is exactly right. You do not correct a word.

events.text: On a hill at dusk you hear a court musician's apprentice practising the old ritual pieces on a bamboo pipe, badly, over and over, the same phrase. On the seventh time, from the pine above, something sings the phrase back, with one note changed. The apprentice stops dead, pipe in the air.

choices.text: Tell the apprentice to play it the bird's way

effects.log: The apprentice plays it the bird's way. It is right; you both know it at once. The apprentice will spend the rest of a long life in the court orchestra trying to hear that note again, and teaching it to everyone, and being told the books say otherwise.

choices.text: Look up into the pine

effects.log: A long tail hangs down through the needles, five colours, and lifts, and is gone. The apprentice did not see it. You decide not to say. Some things are better heard than seen.

events.text: The apprentice of the hill at dusk is the old head of the court orchestra now, and has sent for you. "The note," the old musician says. "I put it in the ninth movement. All these years, and the music masters have struck it out every time. They are rehearsing tomorrow. Will you stand in the courtyard and see if anything comes?"

choices.text: Stand in the courtyard

effects.log: They play it with the note in. At the ninth movement every bird in the palace trees goes silent, and a long shadow crosses the courtyard, and nobody sees what cast it. The old musician, beside you, says only, "There," and is content.

choices.text: Say the note is enough, whether anything comes or not

effects.log: The old musician laughs, and agrees, and plays the note alone on the bamboo pipe that night on the old hill. You hear it from your inn. So, you think, does something else.

events.text: {npc}, a minister of the inner court, has hired you for quiet work: clear the high ridge north of the capital of a pair of birds that sing there. Bird-catchers will do the catching; you will keep them safe. On the minister's eaves, all through the meeting, an owl sits with a dead rat in its claws, and you could swear that when {npc} pauses, the owl talks.

choices.text: Ask {npc} why two birds on a ridge matter

effects.log: "Because they have come to see whether the court is worthy," {npc} says, "and they have been looking at me." On the eaves the owl hisses, and clutches the rat closer. You take the job, to see what it is.

choices.text: Refuse the job

effects.log: You refuse. {npc} does not argue. As you go out of the gate the owl drops down behind you, close enough to brush your hat, and hisses, "Hsss! You want it too! Everyone wants it!" and goes back to its rat.

choices.text: Take the money and warn the birds

effects.log: You take the money. That night you climb the ridge alone and sit under their tree and tell them, aloud, feeling foolish: catchers in three days. In the morning the tree is empty. The catchers find nothing, and {npc} is very angry, and cannot prove a thing.

events.text: On the ridge, at night, with the catchers asleep, the owl from {npc}'s eaves lands on a stump in front of you. It still has the rat. "They want the minister's post," it says, in a voice like a dry hinge. "They want my rat. Everyone wants my rat. Help me keep it."

choices.text: Say, "Hsss!" right back at it

effects.log: The owl is so shocked it nearly drops the rat. It stares at you with enormous eyes and then flies off, muttering. In the morning you tell the catchers the ridge is empty, which by then it is.

choices.text: Ask it what it thinks the birds eat

effects.log: "Rats," it says at once. "Posts. Everything." You tell it: bamboo seed, nothing else, ever. The owl looks at its rat for a long, long time, and then at you, and for the first time seems unsure.

choices.text: Strike the owl down

ok.log: It is faster than an owl and older, and your strike only takes a feather. But it drops the rat as it flees. {npc}, they say, wakes that night shouting about birds.

fail.log: It is not an owl, or not only. It leaves three long scratches across your face and goes back to {npc}'s eaves. (-8 health)

events.text: {npc} has seized the regency. The young king is kept a prisoner in the inner palace. And on the regent's new gate, carved fresh in red and gold, is a phoenix, and the regent's heralds proclaim that heaven's bird has blessed the new order. On the eaves above the carving sits a grey owl, with a rat.

choices.text: Climb up and chisel the carved bird off the gate

ok.log: It takes you one night. By dawn there is a raw patch of wood where the bird was, and the owl is gone, and the whole capital knows what it means: heaven's bird refused the regent. The regency lasts two more years. It feels like less.

fail.log: The guards are waiting. You get the bird's head off before they get you down. A headless phoenix on the regent's gate is, the capital decides, even worse for the regent than none. (-14 health)

choices.text: Go to the ridge and tell the real birds what is being said in their name

effects.log: You tell them. In the morning, in full sight of the capital, two long-tailed birds rise from the north ridge and fly over the regent's palace and on, without stopping, out of the country. Everyone sees. The heralds stop proclaiming.

choices.text: Serve the regent: the order is the order

effects.log: You serve. The owl on the gate watches you go in and out every day, and nods to you, as to a colleague. That is the worst of it.

events.text: {npc}, alchemist of a great sect, has read in an old recipe that a phoenix lays one egg in five hundred years, and that an elixir of it gives a hundred years of life. {npc} has found the nest, high in a paulownia on a cliff, and needs someone of your strength to climb to it. A padded basket is ready. "They will lay another," {npc} says. "In five hundred years."

choices.text: Refuse

effects.log: {npc} shrugs and says there are other climbers. You leave the cave knowing it is true.

choices.text: Agree, and on the cliff, warn the pair instead

ok.log: You climb, and at the nest you find one of the pair sitting on a single red-gold egg, and the other watching from the next branch. You hang there and show them the empty basket, and climb down. That night the nest is empty. They have carried the egg somewhere else, somehow. {npc} never forgives you.

fail.log: The cliff is wet. You fall the last twenty feet and break something in your wrist, and the pair, startled, carry the egg off in the night. {npc} blames you for both the failure and the noise. (-12 health)

choices.text: Agree, and bring the egg

effects.log: You bring it down in the padded basket, warm and red-gold. Behind you on the cliff two voices are crying the whole way. {npc} weighs the egg in both hands with an expression you will see in your dreams.

events.text: The egg is in {npc}'s laboratory, in a nest of silk by the cauldron, and the fire is lit under the cauldron for tomorrow. Tonight the egg has begun to knock from inside.

choices.text: Take it back to the cliff, now

ok.log: You fight your way out of the sect with the egg in your shirt and climb the cliff in the dark. The nest is empty and cold. You put the egg in it and sit on the next branch, and before dawn two shapes come down out of the sky, and one of them settles on the egg as if it had never been gone. The other one looks at you for a long time.

fail.log: You get as far as the sect's gate. There, cornered, you break the egg open with your own hands rather than let it go into the cauldron, and a drab, wet, furious chick tumbles out and runs, and is gone into the dark. You are beaten very badly. You laugh through all of it. (-20 health)

choices.text: Let the alchemy go on

effects.log: The cauldron boils. The elixir, when it is made, does not give a hundred years. It gives nothing at all. {npc} smashes the flask and weeps over the recipe, and you realise you were never told whose recipe it was.

events.text: {npc}, the alchemist, has found another nest, years later, and has hired another climber. You hear of it in a teahouse. The climber is young, hungry and very good.

choices.text: Find the young climber first

effects.log: You find the climber, buy a meal and tell the whole story, the basket, the knocking, the cliff. The young one listens without blinking and says, at the end, "Then I will climb, and come down empty." And does.

choices.text: Go to the cliff and wait under it

effects.log: You wait under the cliff three days. On the third the young climber comes, sees you sitting there, and stops, and the two of you look at each other for a long while. The climber turns round and goes home. You never exchanged a word.

events.text: You have been asked, as the strongest martial artist in the province, to sit beside the new magistrate at a hard hearing: a murim family's land against a village's. In the middle of it, with no wind, a feather comes down out of the clear sky into the courtyard, turning slowly, long as a forearm, five colours, and lands in your open hands. Everyone stares. Far above, two birds are going away east.

choices.text: Put it in your sleeve and go on with the hearing

effects.log: You tuck it into your sleeve as if it were a letter. The hearing goes on. You notice that whenever the murim family's elder speaks, the feather lies cold against your wrist, and whenever the village's old headman speaks, it is warm. You say nothing about that. You do judge accordingly.

choices.text: Give it to the young magistrate

effects.log: You hand it to the magistrate, who is very young and very frightened, and who takes it in both hands as if it were a seal of office. You will hear about this magistrate for years: honest, stubborn, poor, and never once seen without a long feather in one sleeve.

events.text: A powerful sect sends an envoy with a chest of spirit stones and a polite request: in the dispute you have been asked to settle between that sect and a small one, they would be grateful for your understanding. The feather in your sleeve has gone cold as a fish.

choices.text: Send the chest back

effects.log: The chest goes back unopened. You settle the dispute as it should be settled. The feather is warm again by evening. The powerful sect becomes your enemy, politely, for the rest of your life, and you find that you can bear it.

choices.text: Keep the chest and judge fairly anyway

effects.log: You judge fairly; the small sect wins. You keep the stones, telling yourself it changes nothing. The feather stays cold for a year, and when it warms again, it is a little less bright.

choices.text: Open the chest in front of both sects and give it to the small one

effects.log: The powerful sect's envoy turns a colour you have never seen on a face. The small sect's master cannot speak. The story is told in every teahouse in the province, with improvements.

events.text: The young magistrate you gave the feather to, grey now, has been accused of theft from the relief granary by a governor who wants the post for a nephew. The magistrate has sent you no message at all. You hear of it in a teahouse. They say the magistrate holds the feather all through the questioning, and does not speak.

choices.text: Go and speak for the magistrate

ok.log: You stand in the governor's courtyard and tell the story of the feather from the beginning. Halfway through, the governor's own clerk steps forward with the true ledger. The magistrate goes home that evening, the feather in one sleeve, and bows to you at the gate without a word.

fail.log: The governor is not interested in feathers. The magistrate is dismissed, and goes home to a village and teaches children, poor and stubborn and honest, the feather in one sleeve. That, you decide, is not a defeat.

choices.text: Find the true thief yourself

ok.log: It takes a month and a night on a granary roof. The nephew is the thief. The governor resigns, citing ill health. The magistrate never learns who did it, and assumes, with great conviction, that it was the feather.
