fail.log: You find nothing, and the magistrate is dismissed. But on the day the magistrate leaves the county, the whole county lines the road, and the governor watches from a window, and understands something that cannot be taken back.

events.text: The feather in your sleeve has been there more years than you can easily count. It is still five colours. You are thinking, as one does after a long life in the murim, about who should have it after you.

choices.text: Give it to the most honest junior you know

effects.log: The junior refuses, and you insist, and the junior takes it at last as if it were burning. You hear, much later, that it was carried well.

choices.text: Let it go from a high place on a windy day

effects.log: You climb to a peak and open your hand. The feather does not fall: it goes up, turning, and east, against the wind, the way it came. You watch until it is gone.

choices.text: Keep it: it was given to you

effects.log: You keep it. It is not selfishness; you think it was meant to go into the ground with you, as some things are. You sleep better, deciding that.

events.text: The north-east gate of the capital is plagued by birds: every vault and beam is nested, the gate-guards are white with droppings, and the court has ordered a phoenix painted on the vault, the king of birds, to send them elsewhere. The painter has never seen a phoenix and has asked for a guard while working at night, because on the first night something sat on the gate roof and watched.

choices.text: Stand guard, and keep everyone off the gate roof

effects.log: On the third night it comes again: you hear the tiles creak above you, and see the end of a long tail hang over the eave in the lantern light, five colours. The painter, on the scaffold, does not look up and paints faster than ever before. In the morning the bird on the vault looks alive.

choices.text: Tell the painter to come up and look

ok.log: You both climb out onto the gate roof in the dark, and it is there, sitting on the ridge, and lets itself be looked at for as long as it takes to fill a lamp. The painter weeps and paints all night. The little birds leave the gate within the week.

fail.log: The tiles slip and you both nearly fall. When you get to the ridge there is nothing there but the wind. The painter paints a phoenix from memory of a rooster, and the little birds stay.

events.text: Years after the gate was painted, you pass under it. The vault is clean; no bird has nested there since. The painted phoenix is faded, but you could swear it is a little thinner than the day it was painted, as if something real went into the paint, and is still going.

choices.text: Touch the painted feathers

effects.log: The paint is warm under your palm, faintly, like a sleeping animal. A gate-guard sees you do it and says, quietly, that everyone who stood guard that year does the same, and nobody knows why.

choices.text: Pay to have it repainted, carefully

effects.log: The repainter is told to go over the faded colours and change nothing. The repainter, an old hand, says at the end: "I did not have to do much. It was holding itself."

events.text: The king asks you to walk alone in the palace garden at dawn. "Something sits on the roof of the throne hall most mornings," the king says. "The servants are not allowed to look. I know what it is. It has been watching for three years. It has never come down. You can see further than I can. Tell me what it sees."

choices.text: Tell the king the granaries are full and the prisons are not

effects.log: The king listens and says, "And yet it does not come down." You say: perhaps it is still watching the part you cannot see. The king is silent a long time, and that afternoon orders the old records of the last war opened.

choices.text: Say that asking is already a good sign

effects.log: "The kings who do not deserve it," you say, "do not ask me to look. They ask me to bring it down." The king laughs, which you had not heard before. The next morning the tail on the roof is longer: there are two.

choices.text: Say it is not yours to tell, and leave the king to wonder

effects.log: The king nods slowly. "Then I will go on wondering," the king says, "and governing as if it were watching." You think, privately, that this is the whole secret.

events.text: The worthy king is old now, and the springs in the palace courtyard, which were sweet for decades, have started to taste of iron. The crown prince is cruel, and the old king is too tired to stop him. On the throne hall roof at dawn, the two long tails are still there. For now.

choices.text: Tell the old king about the iron in the springs

effects.log: The old king tastes the water and puts the cup down. That month the crown prince is sent to govern a far province with an honest minister at his elbow. The springs do not turn sweet again. But they do not get worse.

choices.text: Go up to the roof at dawn and tell the birds to go before the end

effects.log: You climb to the roof ridge. They are there, and they let you come close. "Go," you say, "while you can still leave as a blessing." They look at each other. The next morning they rise over the capital in full sight and go, and the whole city reads it at once. The crown prince never quite gets the throne.

choices.text: Do nothing: the old king has earned a quiet end

effects.log: You leave it. The old king dies in peace, under two birds on the roof. The new king's reign is short and bad. The birds stay a year into it and then are simply not there one morning, and the springs dry altogether.

events.text: A usurper has taken the capital, and to prove heaven's favour parades through the streets behind a tall pole on which sits a bird: long-tailed, five colours, very still. You are close enough to see the paint on its feathers and the string round its leg. It is a big cock, painted. The painter, they say, is the grandchild of a famous swindler.
events.arc: The King Who Bought a Phoenix

choices.text: Shout the truth from a roof

ok.log: "It is a cock!" you roar from the roof of the rice market, with all your qi behind it. The whole street hears. A child laughs. Then the whole street laughs, the terrible laugh of a crowd that has been afraid. The usurper's reign does not end that day, but it never recovers its dignity.

fail.log: You shout, and the guards are on the roof before the crowd has turned its head. You get away, barely. A few people heard. A few is how things start. (-10 health)

choices.text: Cut the string on its leg as it passes

effects.log: A flick of qi from the crowd and the string parts. The bird on the pole, finding itself free, does what any cock would: it flaps down onto the usurper's palanquin and crows. Paint comes off on the silk. The crowd does not laugh. It does not need to.

choices.text: Let it pass: the real ones will answer for themselves

effects.log: You wait. A month later, in full sight of the capital, two real birds fly over the usurper's palace at noon, and on, without stopping, and are gone. Everyone sees the difference. Nobody says it aloud. Everyone knows.

events.text: The painter of the usurper's cock is in prison, waiting to be blamed for its exposure. You find the painter in a cell, painting birds on the wall with a fingertip and lamp soot. "My grandmother sold a cock as a phoenix once," the painter says, "and got rich from the beating. I only ever wanted to paint the real thing."
events.arc: The King Who Bought a Phoenix

choices.text: Break the painter out

ok.log: You take the painter over the prison wall at night. In the morning you are three counties away, and the painter is already sketching the hills.

fail.log: The prison is better guarded than it looks. You get out alone. A month later the painter is pardoned anyway, in a general amnesty. You decide to call that a success. (-12 health)

choices.text: Promise to take the painter to see the real ones, one day

effects.log: The painter laughs, without hope. But the usurper falls within the year, and the prisons are opened, and the painter comes to find you, with brushes.

events.text: You keep your promise to the painter of the false phoenix: a ridge at dawn, far from any court, where you know two real ones sing. The painter has brought brushes and paper and is shaking.
events.arc: The King Who Bought a Phoenix

choices.text: Sit and wait with the painter

effects.log: They come with the sun. The painter does not paint at all for an hour; just looks. Then paints all day, and the painting, when it is done, has one bird in it and the sign of another, a long second tail coming in from the edge of the paper. "I cannot paint two," the painter says. "Nobody can. You have to show the second one by what it leaves."

choices.text: Leave the painter alone with them

effects.log: You go down the ridge and wait at the bottom. At dusk the painter comes down with paint to the elbows, silent, and you walk all the way back to the town without either of you saying a word.

events.text: The empire of the plains has demanded tribute of the kingdom: horses, silk, ginseng, and a pair of phoenixes. The king, frightened, has agreed. The empire's tribute-takers are already coming up the valley with gilded cages, and the king's ministers have asked you, very quietly, as the one martial artist in the kingdom they cannot order, what you intend to do.

choices.text: Hold the ridge against the tribute-takers

effects.log: You walk up to the ridge with nothing but your sword and sit down under the paulownia where the pair nests. The tribute-takers arrive at noon and find you there. Their captain looks at you for a long moment and decides to make camp and send for orders.

choices.text: Go to the ridge and tell the pair to leave the kingdom

effects.log: You tell them, and they go, that night, over the mountains. The tribute-takers find an empty nest and an empty kingdom in the matter of phoenixes. The king is spared nothing; but the birds are spared everything.

choices.text: Go to the empire's envoy and argue

ok.log: You argue with the envoy for three days: that a phoenix in a cage is a cock in a cage, that heaven's bird cannot be sent, only come. On the third day the envoy, a scholar at heart, writes to the emperor that the phoenixes of the kingdom could not be found. It is the bravest lie you have seen a scholar tell.

fail.log: The envoy listens politely and says that the emperor does not take arguments as tribute. You go to the ridge, then, and sit down under the paulownia, and wait.

events.text: Orders have come back from the empire: take the birds, and take the martial artist who sits under their tree too, if possible, or kill them. The tribute-takers' captain has brought up their best: imperial masters in black, a dozen, with nets of steel thread.

choices.text: Fight them on the ridge

ok.log: It takes from dawn to noon. When it is over the steel nets are in pieces down the scree, and the imperial masters are walking down the valley carrying each other, and the captain is kneeling. Above you, in the paulownia, two birds are singing as if nothing had happened.

fail.deathCause: killed on the phoenixes' ridge by the imperial tribute-takers
fail.log: There are too many, and the nets are made for creatures stronger than you. You go down under them.

choices.text: Hold them while the pair escapes

ok.log: You hold the path for as long as it takes two birds to rise and clear the far mountains. Then you give way, and let the imperial masters past onto an empty ridge, and let them have their laugh at you. It is the best defeat of your life.

fail.log: You hold long enough, barely. The pair clears the mountains. You do not clear the nets, and are dragged a day down the valley before the captain, sick of it, cuts you loose. (-20 health)

choices.text: Negotiate: offer yourself as the tribute instead

effects.log: The captain stares. "A master of your strength, in the emperor's guard, for years," you say, "instead of two birds that will die in a cage." The captain sends the offer. The emperor, amused, accepts. You go west in a gilded cart, and behind you, on the ridge, two voices.

events.text: Ten years in the emperor's guard, as the price of two birds, are over. You come home over the mountains in spring. On the last pass, where the ridge of your kingdom first comes into sight, there is a paulownia you do not remember, young, and in it, singing at dawn, something long-tailed and five-coloured.

choices.text: Sit under it until it finishes

effects.log: It sings until the sun is high. Then it comes down to the lowest branch, the one just above your head, and looks at you, and goes. A second song answers it from the ridge. You walk the rest of the way home without feeling the road.

choices.text: Walk on: you did not do it to be thanked

effects.log: You walk on. Behind you the song stops, and starts again, louder, and follows you for a li down the pass, as if it had something to say and was determined to say it.

events.text: The vassal king who once agreed to send the phoenixes as tribute is dying, and has asked for you. "I would have sent them," the king says. "I was afraid. You were not. Was I a bad king?"

choices.text: Say: a frightened one, which is not the same

effects.log: The king thinks about that for a long time, and nods, and asks you to make sure the next one is less frightened. You say you will try. You do.

choices.text: Say: they would have come to you, if you had asked them instead of the empire

effects.log: The king turns to the window, where the far ridge is just visible, and says nothing more. That night, they tell you later, two birds sat on the roof of the king's sickroom until dawn.

events.text: {npc} is ninety years old, a grandmaster of a famous sword school, and has come up your mountain on foot to ask one thing. "In my youth," {npc} says, "I was never counted among the rising dragons and phoenixes. I was too slow, too poor, too late. They say the best of the young see two birds at dawn before their first great fight. I never did. You are the strongest person I know. Is it too late to be counted?"

choices.text: Fight {npc} at dawn, as if it were a first great fight

ok.log: You fight on the training ground at sunrise, and you do not hold back, and neither does {npc}. In the middle of it {npc} stops dead and looks over your shoulder at the red sky, where two long-tailed birds are passing low, and then laughs, and attacks you again like someone of twenty.

fail.log: {npc} is faster than ninety has any right to be, and you go down in the dew. Lying on your back you see them: two birds going over in the red sky. {npc}, standing over you, sees them too, and sits down on the grass beside you and weeps. (-10 health)

choices.text: Say that the rankings are for the young, and the birds are for everyone

effects.log: {npc} considers that and decides, at ninety, to believe it. You walk down the mountain together. At the bottom, on a paulownia by the road, two birds are sitting, and do not fly when you pass.

events.text: {npc}, the old grandmaster who climbed your mountain at ninety, has died, very old. The sword school has written {npc}'s name, at the family's request, at the end of the list of the rising dragons and phoenixes of {npc}'s generation, decades too late. The other masters are scandalised.

choices.text: Go and sign the list as witness

effects.log: You write your name under the old master's, as witness, in large characters. The scandal stops at once. Nobody wants to argue with your signature. The list is copied into every school's records with the late name in it.

choices.text: Let the masters argue: the old one would have enjoyed it

effects.log: The masters argue for a year. The name stays. You suspect the old one is laughing somewhere, and at dawn on the anniversary, two birds go over the sword school, very low.

events.text: A five-coloured feather is left on your doorstep, and then another, a year apart, and then a third, and you understand at last that it is an invitation. On the highest peak in the east, at the dawn of the summer solstice, the two birds who have been seen over this land for a thousand years are going to rise on the morning sun and not come down. They want a witness who can see that far.

choices.text: Go, and watch to the end

effects.log: You stand on the peak in the dark. At the first light they come up from the valley, together, and do not look at you, and go up into the red sun, and up, until they are a mark on it, and then nothing, and the light is ordinary daylight. You stand there until noon. You have never seen anything so complete.

choices.text: Go, and ask them to stay

effects.log: You ask. One of them lands on the rock beside you and looks at you a long while, kindly, the way one looks at a child who has asked the sun to wait. Then it goes up to its mate, and the two of them go up into the light. You were heard. That is something.

choices.text: Do not go: some things should not have witnesses

effects.log: You stay home. On the solstice morning you are in your yard when the light changes, very slightly, for a moment, as if something in it had been added. You cannot have seen it. You did.

events.text: Since the morning on the eastern peak, scholars keep coming to ask you what you saw, so they can write it in the annals. They want a date, a direction, a sign. The court wants to know whether it means the dynasty is blessed, or finished.

choices.text: Tell them it means nothing for any dynasty

effects.log: The scholars are disappointed and write it down anyway, carefully, without meaning. It is the most accurate entry in the annals for that century.

choices.text: Tell them only the date, and nothing else

effects.log: They write the date. In later centuries people argue about that date the way people argue about stars: everyone sure it meant something, nobody agreeing what. You think that is about right.

events.text: An era of peace is being talked about in the teahouses: the years after the solstice morning, when nothing went wrong anywhere, and nobody can say why. Young people ask you about it, as the one who was there.

choices.text: Say: two birds went up into the sun, and that is all

effects.log: They do not believe you. That is fine. The peace goes on another twenty years, unexplained, which is how peace prefers to be.

choices.text: Say nothing, and smile

effects.log: They decide you are being mysterious on purpose. You are being happy on purpose. From outside, it looks the same.

events.text: You are strong enough now that there is nothing left in the world below you want, except, it turns out, one thing: you would like to hear the phoenixes sing together, once, close. You have heard it from three valleys away. Never close. You know which cliff they sing from at dawn.

choices.text: Go and sit at the foot of their pine, without hiding your strength

effects.log: They know what you are. They sing anyway: one voice and then the other a little behind it, the way the old songs say, the harmony that the court musicians spend their lives failing to write down. It lasts until the sun clears the clouds. You do not open your eyes once.

choices.text: Hide your strength and listen from far off

effects.log: You make yourself small, as small as a person of your strength can, and listen from the next ridge. It is enough. It is more than enough. You go home and cannot speak for a day.

choices.text: Decide not to go: you have had enough of the world

effects.log: You stay home. At dawn, for no reason, from very far, so faint you may be imagining it, you hear two voices, one a little behind the other. You decide not to be sure.

events.text: You hum, without meaning to, at your morning practice: two lines, one a little behind the other. A disciple of another school, passing, stops dead and asks where you learned that.

choices.text: Teach it

effects.log: You teach it, as well as one voice can teach two. The disciple goes away humming it wrong. Two generations later it is a lullaby in three provinces, still wrong, still beautiful.

choices.text: Say you heard it once, from very close

effects.log: The disciple looks at your face for a moment and does not ask anything else. You are grateful.

events.text: The Five Halls of the Patterns stand on a terrace of cloud, each hall named for one of the five characters the old books say are written on the phoenix's body. This is the hall of the head, the hall of virtue. In the first hall, blue as the morning, an old immortal is planting a sapling in a crack of jade, very slowly, and asks you to hold the trowel while the root is set.

choices.text: Hold the trowel, all day if need be

effects.log: It takes all day. The old one does not hurry and does not thank you. At dusk the sapling stands, and you see it is a paulownia, and the old one says only, "Virtue is planting a tree you will not sit under." A mark like a character glows for a moment in the hall's lintel, and fades.

choices.text: Ask the old one what the hall is for

effects.log: "For being asked to hold a trowel," the old one says, "and seeing what you do." You hold the trowel. The answer is in the doing, and in the character that glows in the lintel when the root is set.

events.text: This is the hall of the wings, the hall of righteousness. In the second hall, white as frost, an immortal guard bars your way and says you may pass only if you give up the strongest thing you carry.

choices.text: Give up your weapon

effects.log: You hand it over. The guard looks at it, then at you, and hands it back. "Righteousness," the guard says, "is knowing what you would give up, before anyone asks." A character glows in the lintel.

choices.text: Say the strongest thing you carry is your word, and keep it

effects.log: The guard laughs, and steps aside. "That," the guard says, "is the right answer, and also the most dangerous one. Keep it." A character glows in the lintel.

events.text: This is the hall of the back, the hall of propriety. In the third hall, red as lacquer, a feast is laid for an honoured guest who has not arrived, and a steward begs you to take the guest's seat so the feast is not wasted.

choices.text: Refuse the seat and wait with the steward

effects.log: You wait. The guest never comes. At the end the steward clears the feast and bows to you, the deep bow, and a character glows on the lintel. "Propriety," the steward says, "is not taking the seat that is not yours, even when nobody would know."

choices.text: Take the seat, and serve the steward first

effects.log: You sit, and fill the steward's cup before your own. The steward stares, then laughs, and sits, and the two of you eat the guest's feast together. A character glows on the lintel. You suspect there were several right answers, and that this was one.

events.text: This is the hall of the breast, the hall of benevolence. In the fourth hall, black as deep water, a mortal soul is crying in a corner, lost on the way to rebirth, and has been there a long time, and nobody has stopped.

choices.text: Stop, and walk the soul to the right gate

effects.log: It takes a long time; the soul is very confused and keeps stopping to tell you about a dog it once had. At the gate it turns and thanks you, and goes through. A character glows in the lintel behind you. Benevolence, it seems, is mostly walking slowly.

choices.text: Sit with the soul until it stops crying

effects.log: You sit. It cries, and then talks, and then is quiet, and then gets up by itself and finds its own way. A character glows in the lintel. You had not known that sitting counted.

events.text: This is the hall of the belly, the hall of trust. In the fifth hall, yellow as old gold, there is nobody at all, only a long bridge with no rail over a drop of cloud, and a voice that says the other end is there.

choices.text: Walk across without looking down

effects.log: You walk. The other end is there. A character glows in the lintel, and then all five glow at once, behind you, down the long line of halls, and for a moment you see them for what they are: the five patterns on a bird, the head, the wings, the back, the breast, the belly. Then it is only five halls again.

choices.text: Ask the voice to walk with you

effects.log: Nobody walks with you. But the voice talks to you the whole way, about nothing much, and that is enough to cross on. A character glows in the lintel. Trust, you think, is letting someone talk you across.

events.text: A summons on a strip of cloud: the Court of the Four Spirits asks your testimony. A phoenix is being weighed for its seat, and one of the reigns it graced was a reign you lived under, below, long ago, as a mortal. The court wants to know, from someone who was there: was that ruler worthy?
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Tell the truth: worthy, and flawed

effects.log: You tell it: the good harvests and the bad prison, the fair tax and the cruel war at the end. Hoofprints of light move across the floor of the court as you speak, and stop by you. The record is kept somewhere you cannot see, in a slow hand, by someone very old.

choices.text: Say you were too small then to know

effects.log: "I was a child then," you say. "The rice came or it did not." There is a long silence in the court. Then a voice says that this, too, is testimony, and perhaps the most important kind.

choices.text: Speak for the phoenix instead

effects.log: You tell the court what you remember of the bird, not the king: how it came at dawn, how the spring by your village tasted sweet that whole reign. The court lets you finish. Then a voice, not unkind, says the bird does not need a defender. It needed a witness. You were one anyway.

events.text: After your testimony, a clerk of the Court of the Four Spirits catches you on the cloud steps. "The bird asked who you were," the clerk says. "Not by name. By what you did with your life. It wanted to know whether the people under its reigns turned out well."
events.arc: The Court of the Four Spirits

choices.text: Tell the clerk your life, plainly

effects.log: The clerk writes it all down, the good and the shameful, and rolls it up, and says it will be read. You are surprised how much lighter it feels to have it written by someone else.

choices.text: Say: tell it I turned out

effects.log: The clerk laughs and writes exactly that. You hear, later, that the bird was pleased.

events.text: {npc}, an envoy of the Jade court, wants to know something, and has heard that you lived long enough below to answer it. "In a small kingdom, in a bad century, heaven's omen came down to a king who had done nothing remarkable," {npc} says. "Two birds, at dawn, in full sight. Why that king? The court is not pleased. It suggests the omen is careless."

choices.text: Say: because nothing remarkable is rarer than the court thinks

effects.log: "A king who does nothing remarkable for years," you say, "does not start a war, does not empty a granary, does not hang a minister. Below, that is the most remarkable thing there is." {npc} writes it down, and then sits for a while without writing anything.

choices.text: Say: ask the birds, not me

effects.log: {npc} sighs. "We have. They said what you just said." The envoy rolls up the scroll and goes. You suspect the matter is closed.

choices.text: Ask {npc} what the court considers remarkable

effects.log: {npc} begins a list, and stops halfway, embarrassed. Every item on it is a victory. You do not have to say anything else.

events.text: {npc}, the Jade court's envoy, comes back years later, less severe. "I went down," {npc} says. "To the small kingdom. The king of the omen is long dead. But the spring by the palace still tastes of rice wine, and the villagers still plant paulownias in pairs, and nobody remembers why. I have recommended the court stop asking the birds to explain themselves."

choices.text: Thank {npc}

effects.log: {npc} bows, and you bow, and for a moment you are two old officials on a terrace of cloud who have both learned something late. It is a good moment.

choices.text: Ask whether the court agreed

effects.log: "No," {npc} says, cheerfully. "But it has stopped asking."

events.text: You have been given a small world of the Upper Realm to govern: three cloud-valleys, a few thousand immortals and spirits, a river of light. The old sovereigns tell you there is only one test that matters. If you govern it so well that two birds come, unasked, and stand in the courtyard at dawn, you have done it. Nobody has, for nine hundred years.

choices.text: Govern by not governing: let the valleys be

effects.log: You open the prisons, close the tax office, and sit in the courtyard at dawn. The valleys are confused, then quarrelsome, then, slowly, quiet. It is not enough. But it is a beginning, and you know it.

choices.text: Govern by hard work: every granary, every road

effects.log: You walk every valley and fix every bridge. The valleys prosper. The birds do not come. A spirit of the river, watching you work, says kindly that prosperity is the beginning of the test and not the end.

choices.text: Plant paulownias, and wait

effects.log: You plant a slope of them. The other sovereigns laugh. The paulownias grow, as paulownias do, faster than anyone expected, even in the clouds.

events.text: A dispute in your small world: two cloud-valleys both claim the river of light, and are arming. Your counsellors say you must choose a side quickly, or seem weak. Your paulownias are tall now.

choices.text: Go and sit by the river between the two valleys

effects.log: You sit there for a season and say nothing, and both valleys have to come and talk to you there, by the water they want. They end up talking to each other instead. Nobody arms. It is the hardest thing you have done in a thousand years, and from outside it looks like nothing.

choices.text: Divide the river by your own judgement

ok.log: You divide it so well that each valley is sure it got the better half. That takes a very fine judgement, and a little cunning, and you are not ashamed of either.

fail.log: Both valleys are sure they got the worse half. They do not fight. But they do not forgive you, either, for a century.

events.text: Dawn in your small world, a morning like a thousand others. You go out into the courtyard to sweep it yourself, as you have every morning since you came. There is someone in the courtyard already: two someones, long-necked and five-coloured, standing in a slow measured dance on the stones, as if there were music.

choices.text: Keep sweeping, quietly, around them

effects.log: You sweep around them, and they dance around you, and neither of you makes anything of it. When the sun is up they go. The whole small world saw. Nobody says anything to you about it, ever, which is how you know they understood.

choices.text: Kneel

effects.log: You put down the broom and kneel on the swept stones. One of them stops dancing and comes and stands in front of you, and dips its long neck once, as if in answer to a bow. Then it goes back to its mate, and they finish the dance, exactly, and go.

events.text: {npc}, a sovereign of a rich world of the Upper Realm, has built a palace with a roof of gold and a jewelled perch on its ridge, and wants a pair of phoenixes on it. {npc} has heard that you once saw them dance and wants you to bring them. "I will not take no," {npc} says pleasantly. "Nobody does, these days."

choices.text: Say no anyway

effects.log: {npc} smiles, very slowly. "Then I will find someone who says yes." You have no doubt of it. You also have no doubt how the birds will answer that someone.

choices.text: Explain, patiently, what they will not perch on

effects.log: Only the paulownia. Only bamboo seed. Only a sweet spring. Never a roof, never a cage, never a jewelled perch. {npc} listens with an expression of growing offence, as if the birds had been rude in person.

choices.text: Offer to plant {npc} a paulownia instead

effects.log: {npc} laughs at you. But, the next spring, you hear that a single paulownia has been planted in a corner of the golden courtyard, by night, by someone who did not want to be seen doing it.

events.text: {npc} has caught a bird: not a phoenix, but a great five-coloured pheasant-spirit, dyed brighter, and set it on the jewelled perch, and announced to the Upper Realm that heaven's birds have come to the golden roof. The bird on the perch is miserable. Half the Upper Realm believes it.

choices.text: Free the pheasant-spirit and say why, aloud

ok.log: You break the chain on the perch in front of the whole court. The dyed bird flies off, shedding colour like rain. {npc} says nothing. There is nothing to say. That year, it is said, a paulownia in a corner of the golden courtyard flowered for the first time.

fail.log: {npc}'s guards are many and the golden roof is {npc}'s ground. You are thrown off it. But the chain is cracked, and the pheasant-spirit is gone by morning. (-20 health)

choices.text: Let the Upper Realm judge it for itself

effects.log: You wait. The dye fades in a season. The Upper Realm laughs for a century. {npc}, they say, has stopped receiving guests, and has started, very privately, to garden.

events.text: The village spring has started to taste of rice wine. Not strongly; like the first cup at a wedding, sweet and faintly warm. The old people say it happened once before, eighty years ago, under a good magistrate, and that it means two birds have been drinking there at dawn.

choices.text: Get up before dawn and watch the spring

effects.log: You wait in the pine's shadow. At first light one long-tailed bird comes down and drinks, and then the other, and they look at you, and drink again, as if you were a stone. You carry that morning with you for the rest of your life.

choices.text: Tell the new magistrate about it

effects.log: The new magistrate is very pleased, and has a little roof built over the spring and a stone carved with the date. The water stays sweet for nine years. You try not to think about what that means about the tenth.

choices.text: Fill jars and sell the sweet water in town

effects.log: It sells well. By the third load the water in your jars has gone flat and ordinary, though the water in the spring has not. You stop selling it.

events.text: A new magistrate has come to the county, and the first thing the magistrate does is wall in the sweet spring and sell its water by the cup. The next morning the spring tastes of iron. The magistrate blames the villagers for poisoning it.

choices.text: Tell the magistrate what the sweetness meant

effects.log: The magistrate does not want to hear it, and has you put out of the office. But the next governor's inspector, passing, tastes the iron and asks why, and the villagers all tell the same story. The magistrate is moved on within the year. The water stays iron for ten more.

choices.text: Break the wall down at night

ok.log: It comes down in an hour. The water is still iron. You realise it was never the wall. But the villagers drink from it free again, iron or not, and do not forget who did it.

fail.log: The magistrate's runners catch you with a hammer in your hand. A night in the stocks. It is worth it, you think, though the water is still iron. (-8 health)

choices.text: Wait: magistrates go, springs stay

effects.log: You wait. The magistrate goes, after four bad years. The next is a quiet, honest person. In the second spring of the new term the water is sweet again, and at dawn, you are almost sure, something long-tailed drinks there.

events.text: A master of a fire sect is showing off the sect's great art at a gathering: "the Vermilion Phoenix Rebirth", wings of flame, a death and a rising from the ashes. The crowd roars. Behind the crowd, on a paulownia, a long-tailed bird of five colours is sitting quite still, looking anywhere but at the fire.

choices.text: Point out the bird on the paulownia to the master

effects.log: The master looks, and stops, flames guttering. "That is not fire," the master says, puzzled. No. It is wood, and music, and it does not burn and come back; it ends, like everything. The master looks at the bird a long time and, you hear, renames the art the next year: the Vermilion Bird Rebirth.

choices.text: Watch the bird instead of the fire

effects.log: It is not interested in the fire at all. When the flames die it turns its head to the east and sings once, a cool green sound, like wind in bamboo, and goes. Nobody else noticed.

events.text: Years later, in a southern province, a column of heat and sparks crosses the summer sky at noon, going north, and the paulownias along its path scorch at the edges. That evening the long-tailed bird you once saw at the fire-art gathering is sitting in a scorched paulownia by the road, looking south, very upright, as if after an argument.

choices.text: Bring water and wet the scorched tree

effects.log: You carry water from the stream until the leaves stop curling. The bird watches you do it, and when you are finished, settles its feathers, and sleeps. You have the strange feeling you have just taken a side in a family quarrel.

choices.text: Ask it, aloud, whether the fire was its kin

effects.log: It looks at you. Then it shakes its head, slowly, side to side, exactly like a person, and you laugh out loud on the empty road. It is not fire. It said so.

events.text: Your business takes you into the old throne hall of the palace, empty between audiences. You look up, as everyone does, and there they are, high on the ceiling above the throne: two phoenixes carved among clouds, facing each other, painted red and gold and green. Everyone says they watch the kings. In this light you could almost believe one of them is looking down at you.

choices.text: Look back until you are sure

effects.log: You stand until your neck aches and the light moves. You are never sure. But on the way out an old palace sweeper, who saw you, says that people who look that long at the ceiling come back, always, before they die, and stand there again.

choices.text: Bow, as to elders

effects.log: You bow to a ceiling, in an empty hall. Nobody sees. Something in the gold paint seems, for a moment, to settle, the way a bird settles its feathers.

events.text: A new king has proclaimed an empire, and the painters have been ordered to scrape the phoenixes off the throne-hall ceilings and paint dragons instead, as befits an emperor. You come back to the old hall, the one where you once looked up for so long, and find the scaffolding already going up.

choices.text: Ask the master painter to forget this one hall

effects.log: The master painter looks up at the two carved birds a long while, and then says the scaffolding was put up in the wrong hall by mistake, and has it taken down. This hall is not used for state any more; nobody checks. The phoenixes stay.

choices.text: Help the painters: an empire is an empire

effects.log: You hold the ladder while they scrape. The gold comes down like snow. Behind the paint the wood is bare and pale, and for a moment you see, or think you see, the shape of a wing in the grain. Then the dragons go on.

choices.text: Stand in the hall until the painters give up

effects.log: You stand under the ceiling, saying nothing, for three days. The painters work around you in the other halls, and leave this one till last, and then, for no reason anyone records, never get to it.

events.text: In a year when nothing much goes wrong anywhere, you climb the hill behind the village at dawn for no reason at all, and at the top there are hoofprints in the dew that glow faintly, like a lantern behind paper, and lead away toward the sunrise. Far off a long cloud lies coiled on the horizon like something asleep. You feel, absurdly, that you are late for a meeting of old friends.

choices.text: Follow the hoofprints until they fade

effects.log: They fade at the edge of the hill where the sun comes up. For a moment, standing there, you know exactly where you would sit at that meeting: on the right, between the hoofprints and the cloud, a little above the dark island. Then you are only yourself, on a wet hill, with cold feet and a strange good mood that lasts all year.

choices.text: Sit down and watch the sunrise instead

effects.log: You sit. As the sun clears the hills, two birds cross it, very far off, long-tailed, and are gone. The village below wakes, and quarrels mildly about a fence, and is at peace. You go down and help with the fence.

events.text: In a dream you are standing in a court of clouds as a witness, and a voice asks you, not unkindly, whether the reign you are living under now is worthy. You wake with the question still in your ears.

choices.text: Answer it honestly, in the morning, to yourself

effects.log: You answer it, sitting on the edge of your mat: partly. Good harvests, a cruel tax collector, a fair magistrate, a war on the border nobody explains. Saying it clearly is like cleaning a window. You start, that week, to do something about the tax collector.

choices.text: Answer it by how you live, from now on

effects.log: You decide that the question was for you, not the king. It is a better question that way, and harder. You find yourself, in the years after, being the kind of neighbour a court of clouds could ask about.

events.text: It has been a good year: rain in the right weeks, no fevers, no soldiers on the road. The old people in the village call it "the Phoenix's year", as their grandparents did, and as they say it they look at you, every one of them, for no reason any of them could explain.

choices.text: Ask why they look at you

effects.log: They do not know. One old woman says you have the look of a quiet year about you, whatever that means. You go home and look at yourself in the water jar for a long time and see nothing at all, which, you suppose, is what a quiet year looks like.

choices.text: Go out at dawn and look at the land

effects.log: The paddies are full. The roads are empty of soldiers. A thin light lies over everything in five colours, very faint, and you feel it on your skin like warmth after a long cold. You know, the way you know your own hand, that you have been this light before.

events.text: A quarrel is starting in the market: two families, an old debt, raised voices, a hand on a knife. You walk into the middle of it without deciding to, and stand there.

choices.text: Say nothing, and stand there

effects.log: You say nothing. The voices drop, one by one, as if somebody had laid a hand on each shoulder. The knife goes back into its sheath. Afterwards nobody can say what happened. You cannot either. It is not the first time.

choices.text: Ask them both to come and eat at your house

effects.log: They come, astonished, and eat, and by the end of the meal the debt is halved and forgiven and nobody quite knows how. Peace, you think, is mostly a meal at the right time.

events.text: There is an old throne hall in the palace that is not used for anything now, and you have found an excuse to go in. On the ceiling, among carved clouds, there are two phoenixes facing each other, faded red and gold. You have never been in this hall. You know, before you look, exactly where a crack runs across the left one's wing.

choices.text: Look for the crack

effects.log: It is there, exactly where you knew it would be. You stand under it a long time, with a feeling you cannot name, like coming home to a house where the furniture has been moved a hand's breadth. From up here, you think, you would have seen every king's bald spot.

choices.text: Sit on the steps of the empty throne and look up

effects.log: Nobody stops you. From the throne steps, the two carved birds look straight down, as they looked at every king. You find, sitting there, that you are not afraid of them. You find, more strangely, that you are fond of the kings.

events.text: Carpenters have been sent to repair the old throne hall's roof, and they want to take down the carved ceiling boards, phoenixes and all, to get at the beams. They say the wood is old and the gold is worth something.

choices.text: Pay them to work around the ceiling

effects.log: It takes them twice as long and they grumble the whole time. The phoenixes stay. On the last day the foreman looks up and admits that it would have been a shame. You agree. You would have said more, but you do not know how to say it.

choices.text: Climb up and help them take the boards down whole

effects.log: You take them down with your own hands, slowly, wrapped in cloth, and when the beams are mended you put them back yourself, in the same order. Behind one board, on the bare wood, someone long ago drew a little bird in charcoal. You leave it.

events.text: You are a clerk for a day in a great office, carrying papers, and on the desk of the highest official there lies the seal: old jade, its face carved with two birds facing each other around a flower. Officials come and go and stamp it without looking. You cannot take your eyes off it.

choices.text: Ask the official about the seal

effects.log: "It has outlived six dynasties," the official says, bored. "Whoever holds the highest office carries it. Worthy or not." You hear yourself say, "And every one of them is measured against it." The official looks up for the first time, and goes quiet, and stamps the next paper more slowly.

choices.text: Touch it when nobody is looking

effects.log: The jade is warm. For a moment you are carved into stone, facing someone you love across a flower, and every hand that lifts you is weighed. Then you are only a clerk with ink on your fingers, and someone is shouting for the next file.

events.text: A powerful official wants a document sealed that should not be: a land grant stolen from a village. The seal is on the desk. You are the only one in the room, and the official is waiting outside.

choices.text: Hide the seal until the official goes home

effects.log: You put it in the rice jar in the kitchen. The official storms about for an hour and goes home. In the morning the seal is back on the desk and the land grant has been, mysteriously, mislaid. You never felt so strongly that something was on your side.

choices.text: Seal it: it is not your office

effects.log: You stamp it. The two birds come out on the paper very faint, as if the paste had dried, and you have to stamp it twice. That night you dream of being measured, and found wanting.

choices.text: Take the paper to the highest official yourself

ok.log: The highest official reads it, looks at the seal and at you, and tears the grant in half. "It is measured against it," the old official says, quoting you, it seems, without knowing it.

fail.log: You are thrown out of the office for insolence. But the grant is never sealed, and the village keeps its land. (-6 health)

events.text: You are hired to dig a drainage pit at the ruins of an old temple, and on the third day your spade strikes metal in the mud. You know, before anyone else sees it, what it is: a bronze burner, a mountain of immortals, five musicians, and on top a bird with its wings spread. You know how heavy it is. You know how dark it is down there.

choices.text: Dig it out with your hands, gently

effects.log: You clear the mud away with your fingers, layer by layer. The bird comes up first, gold under the brown, wings open, as if it had been waiting all this time to be dug out exactly like this. The overseer shouts. You hardly hear. You feel your own wings, for a moment, aching from fourteen hundred years of being still.

choices.text: Call the others, and let it be everybody's

effects.log: Twenty people dig it out together, in the rain, laughing and swearing. When it is out, shining, the oldest labourer says it looks like it is about to fly. You say nothing. You think that it already did, once, and chose this.

events.text: The burner from the mud has been set up in a temple hall and lit. Incense smoke comes out between the bronze mountains, and the five bronze musicians seem to move in it. People come from three provinces to see it. You come at night, when nobody is there.

choices.text: Listen to the five musicians

effects.log: There is no sound, of course. But you know the tune they are playing. You hum it under your breath, and the incense smoke, without any wind, leans toward you.

choices.text: Light a stick of incense, and say goodbye

effects.log: You light it and put it in the burner and say goodbye, though you could not say to what. The smoke goes straight up past the bronze bird's wings. You walk out lighter, as if you had put something down at last.

events.text: On the road you pass a village schoolhouse with an enormous paulownia beside it, purple with flowers, and the porch crammed with children chanting their characters. You stop at the gate and cannot go on. You know the tree. You know, somehow, the shape of the window it looks into, and the lamp that used to burn there late.

choices.text: Go in and ask about the tree

effects.log: The teacher says a poor scholar planted it long ago to see the phoenix and died waiting, and that the spring after the scholar died, two birds came and never left, and that the school has never lacked students since, and nobody has ever dared cut the tree. The teacher says all this as if it were obvious. To you, it is.

choices.text: Sit under the tree and listen to the lesson

effects.log: You sit in the shade and listen to the children get their characters wrong. A purple flower falls into your lap. You feel, quite clearly, that you came too late once, and stayed, and that staying was right.

events.text: The village schoolhouse with the great paulownia needs a teacher: the old one has died, and nobody will come so far for so little. The headman, who remembers you sitting under the tree, writes to ask.

choices.text: Go and teach, for a few years

effects.log: It is the poorest pay of your life and the best years. Every spring two birds sing in the paulownia at dawn, and every spring a few more children come. When you leave, you plant a paulownia by the gate, for whoever teaches next.

choices.text: Send money, and find them a teacher

effects.log: You find a young scholar who failed the examinations twice and is ashamed, and send them. You hear, later, that the young scholar never left, and was never ashamed again.

events.text: The road takes you through a small hill country below a green mountain the local people call Bibong, the flying phoenix, because, they say, a phoenix rose from it one morning long ago and then settled there for good with its mate, and the country has been lucky ever since. You have never been here. Your feet know the paths.

choices.text: Climb to the top at dawn

effects.log: You climb in the dark without a lantern and do not stumble once. At the top, as the sun comes up, you open your arms without meaning to, and the wind comes up the slope under them, and for a moment your whole body remembers rising. You come down slowly, and the country below looks like a home you left on purpose.

choices.text: Ask the villagers what they do to keep their luck

effects.log: "Nothing," an old farmer says. "That is the trick. We took the nets down long ago. We plant paulownias. We do not ask." You find yourself nodding, as if you had told them that yourself, once.

events.text: A lord of the hill country below Bibong, newly come to power, has ordered nets strung on the mountain, "to keep the luck in". The villagers are frightened and angry. Somebody remembers the stranger who climbed the mountain in the dark, and comes to find you.

choices.text: Go and take the nets down yourself

ok.log: You cut them all in one night, as somebody did once before, long ago, though you cannot say how you know that. At dawn the lord's men find cut silk and a singing mountain. The lord is wise enough to leave it.

fail.log: The lord's guards catch you halfway. You are beaten and thrown off the mountain. But half the nets are down, and the villagers finish the rest the next night, all of them together. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go to the lord and tell the story of the mountain

effects.log: You tell it as if you were there. The lord listens with a strange face, and at the end asks how you know all this. You say you do not know. The nets come down that week.

events.text: The morning of your first great fight, a duel that will decide whether your name goes on the list of the rising dragons and phoenixes. You are up before dawn, too frightened to eat. As the sky turns red, two long-tailed birds go over the training ground, very low, and one of them turns its head on its long neck and looks at you as it passes, like a teacher checking a student's stance.

choices.text: Straighten your stance

effects.log: You straighten it, without thinking. The bird looks away, satisfied, and goes. You fight that afternoon better than you have ever fought, and when your name goes on the list, it feels less like winning than like being recognised by someone who has known you a long time.

choices.text: Bow to them

effects.log: You bow, on the empty training ground, to two birds. Your opponent, arriving, sees you do it and laughs. You win anyway. The laugh, you notice, did not bother you at all.

events.text: You are older now, and a young fighter from a poor school, with no name and no patron, has come to ask you to watch their first great fight. Nobody else will come. The fight is at dawn.

choices.text: Go, and stand where the young one can see you

effects.log: You stand at the edge of the ground at sunrise. Just before the fight the young one looks up at the red sky, and you see two long-tailed birds pass over in the young one's eyes before you see them in the sky. You do not say anything. You do not need to.

choices.text: Train the young one for the month before

effects.log: You train them hard for a month, mostly in stance. On the morning of the fight you notice you have taught exactly the way a long-necked bird once looked at you. The young one wins, and goes on the list, and comes to thank you, and cannot quite say for what.

events.text: The rising dragons and phoenixes of this generation are announced in the market square. You are too old, or too young, or too obscure to be on the list, and do not care. But when the herald reads out the old words that begin it, "named for the dragon and the phoenix, who were young once", you find you are crying.

choices.text: Stay and hear every name

effects.log: You stay and hear every name. Each one you wish well, quietly, as if they were your own chicks. A child beside you asks why you are crying. You say: because they are all so young. The child does not understand. You hope the child never has to.

choices.text: Go home, and practise at dawn

effects.log: You practise in the yard at sunrise. Nobody is watching. You are not on any list. It is the best morning of practice in your life.

events.text: At sunrise, for no reason, you stop in the middle of the field and look straight into the red sun, and your hand comes up by itself, reaching, as if to take someone's hand who should be beside you. There is nobody. The old people say this land had a great peace once, long ago, after two birds flew into the sunrise and did not come down.

choices.text: Leave your hand there a moment longer

effects.log: You leave it there. For a moment it is not empty: something holds it, light and certain, the way a wing holds air. Then the sun is up and you are a person in a field with a hand in the air. You put it down, and are not sad at all.

choices.text: Ask the old people about the peace

effects.log: They tell it the same way every time: nothing happened. No war, no famine, nobody remarkable. Nobody can say why. Their grandparents just remembered two birds going up into the morning. You listen as if to a story about someone you were very close to.

events.text: You have never been good at being alone. Not lonely: alone. Everything you do, you do as if someone were beside you, a little behind, like the second voice in a song. This year you meet someone who walks exactly that way, a little behind, on your left.

choices.text: Walk with them

effects.log: You walk with them all that spring and do not talk much. You do not need to. Whatever becomes of it, you know now what the shape beside you was for.

choices.text: Let them go, and keep the shape

effects.log: You let them go their way. The shape beside you stays. It is not empty, you decide. It is kept.

events.text: Every child in the country learns three lines by an old scholar, about planting a paulownia to see the phoenix, and the phoenix never coming, and only the bright moon hanging on the empty branch. You learned them too, as a child, and could never say them aloud without your throat closing. Tonight, walking home, you pass a bare paulownia with the moon in it.

choices.text: Stop and say the lines to the tree

effects.log: You say them, and your throat closes, as always. But this time you say them to the end. Something in the branch stirs, very faintly, though there is no wind: a single long feather, caught in the twigs, turning in the moonlight. You leave it there. It was waiting for somebody, and it was not you; it was the one who never came back.

choices.text: Walk past quickly

effects.log: You walk past without looking. At home you sit by the door until the moon sets, and you cannot have said why, and you do not sleep.

events.text: A neighbour has lost a spouse of forty years, and sits every evening under a tree in the yard, not eating, looking at the place where the other one used to sit. The family is frightened. They have asked you, because you are the one who always seems to know what to say about grief, though you have never told anyone why.

choices.text: Sit with the neighbour, and say nothing

effects.log: You sit under the tree every evening for a month. On the last evening the neighbour says, "I have to go on for both of us, don't I?" and you say yes, and the neighbour eats for the first time in a month. You go home and cry for an hour, for someone you have never met.

choices.text: Tell the neighbour to make a vow: to keep going, for both

effects.log: "Make a vow," you say, "at the place where they last sat. Not to forget. To go on." The neighbour stares at you, and then does it, aloud, in the yard. You do not know where the words came from. You only know that somebody, once, did not make that vow, and should have.

events.text: In the market you pass a poultry yard full of hens pecking millet, and stop so suddenly that someone walks into you. Among the hens is a big dull bird with a long, bedraggled tail, standing apart, not eating. The poultry seller laughs and says a swindler once sold one like that to a magistrate as a phoenix. You cannot laugh. You find you cannot look at millet.

choices.text: Buy the bird and let it go on a hill

effects.log: You carry it to the nearest hill and set it down under a pine. It does not fly; it walks off into the undergrowth like any chicken. It is only a chicken. You stand there a long time anyway, because somebody, once, was not.

choices.text: Ask the seller to tell the swindler story

effects.log: The seller tells it well: the swindler, the magistrate, the beating, the money back. Everyone laughs. You smile, and keep smiling, and go home and do not eat millet again for the rest of your life, and nobody understands why.

events.text: Someone offers you a bargain too good to be true: a little dishonesty, a little profit, nobody hurt. Your whole body refuses before your mind has finished hearing it, the way some people's throats close at the smell of a food that once made them ill.

choices.text: Trust the refusal

effects.log: You refuse. You cannot explain why to the person offering, or to yourself. Later you hear the bargain ruined three families. You do not feel clever. You feel, very strongly, that you once learned this at a terrible price, and that it stuck.

choices.text: Override it, just this once

effects.log: You take it. It works. You are richer. That night you dream of a dusty yard and hens, and of forgetting something important, and you wake with the taste of millet in your mouth.

events.text: Before an old palace gate stands a tall pole with an empty gilded cage at the top, rusted, and a faded banner painted with two birds. The old people spit when they pass it. A tyrant once kept heaven's bird in that cage, they say, and brought it out at every coronation to prove heaven's favour, and the people learned to curse two birds on a banner. You cannot walk past it. Your chest is tight as a bound wing.

choices.text: Climb the pole and break the cage open

ok.log: The rusted door comes away in your hand. The cage is empty, has been empty for centuries. You throw the door down into the street anyway, and the old people below, who spat at the pole every day of their lives, stop, and do not spit, and one of them bows.

fail.log: The pole is slick and old and you fall the last part. The guards laugh at you. You do not care. You go back the next night and try again. (-6 health)

choices.text: Ask the old people not to curse the birds, but the cage

effects.log: They look at you strangely. One old man thinks about it and says you are right: the bird did not ask for the cage. He stops spitting. A few of the others do too. It is a small thing. It feels like a great one.

events.text: A new ruler's coronation, and the heralds are proclaiming heaven's favour: signs, omens, a lucky star, birds seen over the palace. Everyone around you is cheering. You feel sick.

choices.text: Say, loudly, that omens can be bought

ok.log: A few people hear and stop cheering and think. One of them, you learn later, becomes a censor, and writes in a famous memorial that a ruler must be measured by the granaries, not the birds.

fail.log: The crowd turns on you, and a guard's staff finds your ribs. You go home and sit with the bruise and do not regret it. (-8 health)

choices.text: Watch the new ruler, not the omens

effects.log: You stop listening to the heralds and watch the ruler's face. It is tired, and afraid, and not cruel. You decide to wait and see. That, you think, is all any bird should ever have done.

events.text: In the old capital of a fallen kingdom there are great round mounds of earth, grassed over, the size of hills. Children slide down them. You climb one, and at the top the ground sways under your feet like the deck of a ship, and you sit down hard, sick to your stomach. Nobody else feels anything.

choices.text: Lie down on the mound and let it pass

effects.log: You lie on your back with your arms out. The swaying goes on, slow and huge, the whole land rolling like a boat in a swell, and you know without being told that you sat here once, on an egg that could never hatch, out of loyalty, while everything went down. Then it stops. You are on a grassy hill, and a child is asking if you are ill.

choices.text: Go and look for the well in the chestnut grove

effects.log: You walk straight to it, through streets you have never seen: an old well, choked with leaves, in a grove of chestnuts by the river. You sit on its edge until dark and do not know whether you are angry or sad. In the end you decide it was neither the well's fault nor yours.

events.text: The house you serve is failing: debts, a bad heir, a feud it cannot win. Everyone else has quietly found other employment. You stay, out of old loyalty, and every night you dream of the ground swaying like a ship.

choices.text: Leave, in daylight, and say why

effects.log: You go to the head of the house and say, plainly, that you are leaving and why, and walk out of the front gate at noon. The heir, shaken, sells the feud and pays the debts. The house does not sink. Leaving in sight, it turns out, was the most loyal thing you could do.

choices.text: Stay to the end

effects.log: You stay. The house goes down, slowly, and you with it, and come out the other side poorer and alive. You do not regret it, exactly. But the next time, you think, you will know the swaying for what it is, sooner.

events.text: In a king's treasury, on a feast day when the doors are open, you see it: an ancient gilt-bronze crown from a hill kingdom long gone, its standing ornaments set with feathers, faded but still five colours. People say it is priceless. You put your hand to your own shoulder, where it hurts suddenly, as if something had been plucked.

choices.text: Stand before it as at a grave

effects.log: You put your hands together and stand there until the keeper asks you to move on. You do not know whom you are mourning. You only know that the crown is beautiful, and that you wish with your whole body it had never been made.

choices.text: Ask the keeper where the feathers came from

effects.log: "Pheasant, dyed," the keeper says, and then, seeing your face, lowers the voice: "Some say not. Some say there was a bird once that the feather-takers took. Nobody likes to say it on a feast day." You thank the keeper and go out into the sun and stand very still.

events.text: In the hills, you come across the camp of feather-takers: a mirror propped against a pine, a dish of millet, a long net. Your hands are shaking before you understand why.

choices.text: Break the mirror and scatter the millet

ok.log: The takers come back to find their mirror in pieces and you sitting on their net. There is a short fight, which you win. You burn the net. You do not know why it feels like settling an old account. It does.

fail.log: There are more of them than you thought. But the mirror is broken before they reach you, and a mirror-trap without its mirror catches nothing that season. (-10 health)

choices.text: Wait on the ridge and warn whatever comes

effects.log: You wait all night on the ridge above the trap. At dawn, two long-tailed shapes come over the far peak. You stand up and wave your arms like a fool, and shout, and they turn, and go round the other side of the mountain. You sit down and laugh until you cry.

events.text: On a mountain in the south the rock is veined with gold and jade, and a stream runs red with cinnabar. You shelter from the rain in a cave and the sand under you is red. Your hands start digging before you have decided to. A finger's depth down there is an egg, red-gold and faintly warm, and you know, the way you know your own name, that it remembers everything.

choices.text: Cover it again, gently, and keep the rain off it

effects.log: You heap the red sand back over it and sit at the cave mouth all night with the rain on your back. In the morning you go, and do not tell anyone where. Somewhere far off, you are sure, there is another egg. It is not your business to find it. It will find its own way.

choices.text: Sing to it, though you do not know the song

effects.log: You sing. You do not know the tune, and you sing it anyway, and your voice does something it has never done, a little behind itself, as if it were two voices. The egg is warmer under your palm when you stop. You leave it in the sand and go out into a rinsed morning.

events.text: Years after the cave on the cinnabar mountain, a drab, loud, ungainly young bird lands on your windowsill at dawn and screams at you. It is mostly beak. One of its feathers, just one, has turned blue.

choices.text: Laugh, and let it scream

effects.log: It screams until the sun is up and then, in the silence after, sings and dances on the sill by itself, awkward and very serious, for nobody. Then it flies off east. You are laughing for an hour.

choices.text: Put out a dish of millet, and see

effects.log: It looks at the millet with total contempt and flies away. You are absurdly proud of it.
